items.fullDescription: This ACLA seminar asks what it means to teach the "world" in fields such as world cinema, world literature, comparative literature, and global media studies. Courses organized around the world often promise breadth, diversity, and cross-cultural understanding, but they also face practical and conceptual problems. What counts as the world? How does the nation appear in "world" courses? How do syllabi balance coverage, depth, translation, historical context, aesthetics, and political urgency? How do institutional expectations and restrictions mold the student imagination of the "world"? How does the positionality of the instructor presuppose, structure, or influence the "world" classroom? The seminar invites papers on the pedagogy of world cinema, media, literature, and related fields. We welcome reflections on syllabus design, classroom practice, study abroad programs, canonicity, national, regional, and transnational frameworks, diaspora, migration, colonial and postcolonial histories, language, accessibility, and the politics of curation. Participants might address how a single course constructs the world, how students respond to unfamiliar forms and contexts, how films or texts travel across classrooms, or how teaching the world changes across institutional locations. Through the discussions generated by this seminar, we hope to gather strategies for reimagining "world" courses in film, literature, and new media classrooms. Therefore, this seminar is especially interested in approaches that treat pedagogy as a site of theory. How do teaching practices revise our understanding of the world itself? What models of the world do our classrooms reproduce, and what alternative worlds might they make possible? We welcome both theoretical reflections and concrete case studies, including discussions of specific courses, syllabi, assignments, classroom practices, films, texts, or teaching contexts. Submit your proposal through this link: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6f456f04-ac0e-4024-9daf-ec6a4ca3e277

items.fullDescription: How do writing and general education programs create conditions for communities that empower themselves-sustaining, growing, and often exceeding their original design? This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular interest in work that attends to the unexpected: encounters, connections, and forms of growth that arise when pedagogy exceeds the transactional to become genuinely communal. Papers might address-for example-embedded tutoring or near-peer mentoring in composition; teaching-and-learning communities (communities of practice) among faculty, tutors, and students; writing or Gen Ed programs at HSIs, HBCUs, or open-access institutions; the relationship between first-year instruction and identity transformation; intergenerational writing communities and alumni engagement; or the challenges that AI poses to authentic intellectual and creative development. Empirical, theoretical, and reflective approaches are welcome, as is work that bridges composition pedagogy, approaches to general education, and literary (or other forms of) community-building.

items.fullDescription: From Christopher Strachey's Love Letter Generator to today's generative AI writing tools and multimodal models, AI technologies are reshaping how literary works are created, adapted, and circulated across media. Texts can now be generated, illustrated, voiced, animated, and transformed into comics, audiobooks, visual art, and video, prompting renewed questions about creativity, form, authorship, authenticity, and human agency. This seminar asks: Can AI-generated literature and art be understood as forms of artificial creativity? Does AI expand, automate, or redefine human creativity? How does human-AI collaboration challenge traditional ideas of authorship and authenticity? How do generative technologies reshape intertextuality, intermediality, and the boundaries between literature and other art forms? What methodological problems arise when AI is used to analyze AI-generated literature? And how do readers, critics, publishers, and institutions respond differently to AI-generated works across literary genres and fields? We welcome papers on AI-generated literature and multimodal works, human-AI collaboration, authorship and creativity, AI-assisted literary research, intertextuality and intermediality, and literary or artistic representations of AI. To submit a paper proposal, please visit the ACLA seminar page and click "Propose a Paper": https://www.acla.org/seminar/dfc44a1b-7299-4016-a661-6095054a6917 Submission deadline: September 20, 2026. items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. items.fullDescription: Call for Papers NeMLA 2027 Annual Convention Rethinking the Fantastic: Impossibility, Ontology, and Alternative Realities What makes a text fantastic? While traditional definitions often emphasize the supernatural or the uncanny, many literary works generate the fantastic through impossibility itself. Impossible worlds, contradictory realities, unstable identities, infinite spaces, and paradoxical temporalities challenge readers' assumptions about reality and invite new ways of understanding existence. This panel explores the fantastic through the lens of impossibility, examining how literature constructs alternative realities that disrupt conventional notions of ontology, epistemology, identity, language, memory, and time. While the work of Jorge Luis Borges serves as a significant point of departure for these discussions, the panel also welcomes comparative and interdisciplinary approaches that extend beyond Borges to other literary traditions, periods, and media. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Impossibility as a defining feature of the fantastic Ontological and epistemological uncertainty Borges and the redefinition of the fantastic Comparative studies of Borges and other writers of the fantastic Alternative realities, dreams, simulations, and virtual worlds Labyrinths, infinite libraries, mirrors, doubles, and paradoxes Time, memory, identity, and narrative impossibility Metafiction and self-reflexive narrative The fantastic across cultures, languages, and historical periods Philosophical approaches to the fantastic Contemporary fantasy, speculative fiction, and science fiction in relation to impossibility We welcome proposals from scholars at all career stages and encourage contributions from literary studies, comparative literature, philosophy, cultural studies, media studies, and related disciplines. Submission Information Please submit a 250-300-word abstract through the NeMLA submission portal. Submission deadline: September 30, 2026 CFP page: https://cfplist.com/nemla/ Home/S/22693 Session modality: Remote only This panel seeks to foster conversations on how impossibility reshapes our understanding of the fantastic across literary traditions and theoretical perspectives. We look forward to receiving proposals that reconsider the fantastic beyond conventional boundaries. abeler17@posta.pau.edu.tr Ayse Nur Beler

items.fullDescription: This panel invites participants to enlarge on the theoretical, scholarly, and humanistic aspects of community building. Beginning with the idea that the humanities are about nurturing community when so much in our world seeks to drive us apart, we will consider such life-giving functions of humanistic scholarship as fostering joy, facilitating healing, being part of the natural world, and engaging the physical senses and the life of the body. These concerns rarely abide by the expectations of any one academic discipline, field, or department. The more "silo'd" our learning, the less serviceable we are to the actual life of humanity. A wise social-scientist friend of mine recently shared with me that it's considered animal cruelty to own just one duck because they're intrinsically social creatures--a telling reminder that it's not our fault that we ourselves do so badly isolation, yet just the kind of knowledge we tend to foreclose in an average humanities classroom. Likewise, my own training as a woodworker shapes my understanding of the material as well as the intellectual and emotional foundations of my life in queer community. Hence, this panel encourages views of humanistic practice that refuse narrow disciplinary boundaries, and dispensing with limiting assumptions about the potential of academia to take part in a thriving world. For my own part, I will talk about the centrality of reading groups in my own life-not only the well-known sort in which participants discuss something they've all read, but in which we take turns reading aloud to one another, for the sonorous, material, physical, voice-lifting joy of it. (Needless to say, the text has to be worth it; this is not a book-of-the-month kind of approach). Participants will be encouraged to write about and share the sources of wisdom that guide their own efforts to build and sustain community. Suggested topics include ancestral and indigenous wisdom on community relations; pedagogical, philosophical, and poetical approaches to learning in community; performance practices linking music, poetry, and other formally disparate media; liberatory approaches to education; communities of reading and interpretation; the ethics of finance; and the intersection of community and creativity.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / COLLEGE ENGLISH ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONFERENCE APRIL 1-3, 2027 / ST LOUIS, MO SUBMISSION SITE IS OPEN: https://www.conftool.pro/cea2027 DEADLINE: 11/01/2026 For its 2027 annual conference,the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. we also encourage proposals on GENERAL TOPICS, including AMERICAN, BRITISH, AND WORLD LITERATURES. DON'T KNOW CEA? YOU SHOULD! In December 1938, a group of young academics attending the MLA convention in New York took on the biggest name in their field-the MLA. They chose to forge a new path by organizing into the College English Association and offering a voice to "the college English teachers of America." Their aim was to upend the scholar-teacher dynamic by recognizing teaching as paramount. Today, more than eight decades later, the CEA continues in that same spirit. At our core, we strive to meet these goals through two venues: our Annual CEA Conference and our journal, The CEA Critic. With over 400 active members and a collection of regional affiliates, the CEA welcomes teacher-scholars at all levels-from graduate students to emeritus faculty-who share our belief that teaching is central to who we are and what we do. CEA WELCOMES GRADUATE STUDENTS As always, the CEA extends a special invite to students pursuing a graduate degree, not only to attend the conference but to submit their presentations to the CEA Outstanding Graduate Student Paper competition. The award carries a grand prize of $250 and publication of the winning essay in the CEA's flagship journal, THE CEA CRITIC. NEW FOR 2027:UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island Roundtable Title: Writing and Wellbeing: A New Urgency for Human-Centered Composition Pedagogies Primary Area / Secondary Area: Rhetoric & Composition / Pedagogy & Professional Modality: In person only Chair: Miranda Lutyens, University of Massachusetts Amherst College is a time of excitement and novelty, but it can also bring about anxiety and uncertainty. Those unsettling emotions have been on an upward trend in recent years, with a host of factors - the fallout of the pandemic, social media's curation of idealized lives, and existential fears relating to climate change, generative AI, and political turmoil - raising concerns about the wellbeing of students. The college writing classroom has a long history of offering compassion through creative (and even countercultural) approaches to teaching and learning. This included affirming the rights of linguistically marginalized students to their own language, as well as efforts to keep struggling writers in school to keep them out of the Vietnam War. As we collectively face new urgencies, this roundtable session invites participants to share research projects and instructional practices that consider college writing classrooms as affective and embodied spaces. Recognizing concerns such as instructors' emotional labor and under-resourced writing programs, the session primarily focuses on putting forward innovative approaches to making writing instruction responsive to students' experiences in increasingly uncertain times. Insights gained from critical teacher research on human-centered pedagogies are particularly welcome, as are contributions from all levels of writing instruction, including first-year composition, writing in the disciplines, writing support for graduate students etc. The goal of this roundtable is for both participants and attendees to leave with expanded perspectives on how the college writing classroom might offer students more pleasure and new possibilities - to reimagine a more salutary relationship to writing, to engage with the written word in more personally meaningful ways, and to gain a greater awareness of themselves and others. The roundtable also aims to offer practical strategies for enacting - or at least experimenting with - new classroom practices. items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). Papers in STEM fields that clearly articulate relevance to the theme are welcome. Full-panel proposals will be given priority. Panel proposals must include a 200-250 word proposal for the panel in addition to abstracts for each individual participant. A select number of travel grants will be awarded on a competitive basis for those traveling more than 100 miles. To qualify for a travel grant, you must submit your application by August 14, 2026. Further details will be included in your registration sign-up. Please submit abstracts via the following google form link: https://tinyurl.com/2026ERAH

items.fullDescription: Accepting Submissions for NeMLA Roundtable: In this in-person roundtable conference session, we are looking to open conversation about the unique ways that educators are innovating with forms of gaming, play, and playfulness in the classroom. We are interested in discussing the incorporation of any and all forms of games and gaming, including, but not limited to: - board, tabletop, and card games - social deduction games - tabletop role-playing systems such as Dungeons and Dragons - invented role-playing scenarios - gamification of in-class activities - video and digital games Abstract / Overview Tabletop gaming and literary studies share a core essence: storytelling. As we aim to teach students in our writing, rhetoric, composition, and literature courses the values and techniques of narrative, we might choose to borrow from the myriad strategies developed in the world of board and role-playing games in order to engage learners on an even more visceral level. Applying approaches of play and pretend, whether through published or in-class created gaming scenarios, educators can enable rich modes of experiential learning. Such learning has the potential to bond our classroom communities more profoundly than verbal chatter alone may accomplish-and, perhaps, to undergird our intrinsic human need to build shared, lived encounters in ways that machines and AI cannot simulate. items.fullDescription: Addiction is strongly associated with what Jacques Derrida termed "our narcotic modernity," to the point of being synonymous with its ills--even, or especially, as both addiction and modernity flicker between their narrowest and broadest senses. On one hand, according to an influential Foucauldian line of thought, addiction as an identity and an institutional formation dates to the nineteenth century, when certain kinds of drug use, much like certain kinds of same-sex intimacy, were pathologized by medicine and criminalized by law. At the same time, addiction's challenges to subjecthood and agency--and its extension as a model for everything from shopping to smartphone use--have made it a powerful figure for capitalist modernity's effects on the self. Taken together, these accounts of addiction as specifically modern and modernity as generalized addiction render the two terms at once interdependent and unstable, a problem of definition running parallel to the urgent social problems of addiction and its failed carceral solutions. Building on recent scholarship by Jennifer Fleissner, Rebecca Lemon, and others, we seek to retheorize addiction and its periodization through a wider view of its articulation across different eras and contexts. This seminar seeks to bring together scholars working at the intersection of addiction and literature from the premodern to the postmodern, to reconfigure our understanding of how these concepts are negotiated and narrativized across time. How has the concept of addiction changed over time, and how have these shifting conceptions been represented in literary terms? How can a critical examination of addiction narratives reconfigure our concept of "modernity"? Is addiction literature a distinct mode? What does addiction look like in the present, and in contemporary literature? What norms, histories, and assumptions overdetermine its representation? Crucially, what do these changes mean in practice-that is, how do they impact our cultural understanding of addiction and how our society treats those living with it? The stakes of these questions are particularly high in the context of a society grappling with the ongoing opioid crisis and related debates about harm reduction, who is deserving of care, empathy, and self-determination, and what we owe to one another as members of a human community. Potential topics include (but are not limited to): Free will, self-possession, agency, and self-control Capitalism, consumption, and commodity fetishism Narratives of slavery and enslavement Literary forms and genres associated with addiction: allegory, picaresque, memoir, trip report, confessional, cautionary tale, body horror, etc. Character theory and the "Addict" (character systems and economies, depth and typicality, etc.) The individual body and the social body Shifting narratives of subjecthood and the Self Medicalization and moralization of addiction Shifting approaches to conceptualizing and treating addiction Submit abstracts directly through the ACLA seminar portal: https://www.acla.org/seminar/8d51e4c4-9c0f-4b74-85e5-5d43ca66fdc3

items.fullDescription: Papers with a specifically comparative focus on the sins of reading (Peccata Lectionis) can examine the topic of the seminar from a theoretical, methodological and thematic perspective. If we speak about the event of reading in a general sense, misreading as an interpretative act should not necessarily be defined as a sin or even as a mistake. At least, this cannot be done as clearly as in a legal, ethical or psychological discourse about sin or a mistake in the case of a Mozart overture played out of tune. What then is the sin of reading? From a theoretical point of view, it may well be defined as a complement to "the virtue of reading" (Virtus Lectionis, Ambrus 2026). All this creates a connection between the literary canon and canonisation known from the Christian religious tradition, and perhaps the sin of reading lies in non-canonical interpretation. Also, literary critics as professional readers can commit one of the sins of reading when losing their credibility with lay people watching them. However, the most radical theoretical and methodological problem stems from language itself. If we give credit to Nietzsche's philosophical claims on language adopted from Gustav Gerber, we must also consider language itself and hence literature as an accumulation of errors, in accordance with Paul Ricoeur's theory of metaphor, identifying the origin of tropes as linguistic errors. The professional reading of literature, which is considered as a set of mistakes, is already lying when it discusses its subject not as rhetorical errors, but as aesthetic quality. When we study the literary works of different cultures and periods and think about the sins related to reading, we can come to a similar conclusion. The seminar welcomes any comparative and even interdisciplinary paper that wants to take into account the above problems of reading, primarily in association with the Judeo-Christian tradition and sin understood according to Western philosophical concepts. From a literary point of view, special attention may be paid to the works of Aristophanes, Dante, Cervantes, Laurence Sterne, E. T. A. Hoffmann, Henry James, Marcel Proust, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce, Jorge Luis Borges or Paul Auster, and from a religious point of view, to the works of Philo of Alexandria, the Kabbalist thinkers, Origen, Saint Augustine, Hugh of Saint Victor, Ticonius, Rudolf Bultmann, Northrop Frye, Gershom Scholem, and David Tracy.

items.fullDescription: The construction of archives has long been a fraught process that brings dominant ways of knowing, which are often Western and colonial, into conflict with cultural knowledge. Despite recent efforts to decolonize institutions and collections, many archival practices were developed in ways that contribute to this tension while introducing ethical and epistemological questions that complicate our ability to read archives as authoritative collections. Decisions about selection, description, curation, organization, and exhibition have vital implications for access and the construction of narrative within the archive. By questioning these practices as a series of choices and attitudes, scholars can arrive at a more meaningful understanding of how they enable and frustrate different kinds of knowledge production. This panel invites proposals that explore past and present archival practices to consider how they impact and empower knowledge communities. We invite papers from a variety of disciplinary perspectives, and welcome work that engages with a diverse range of material and digital objects. What kinds of knowledge choices are curators, collectors, and educators making? How are researchers and students interacting with these archival materials in ways that reinforce and challenge Western epistemologies? How do the ways that publics access and interact with archival collections and exhibits shape cultural knowledge and memory? How does a lack of access condition or obstruct agency in ways that constrain social change? Please submit a 250-300 word abstract through the NeMLA portal for consideration. Contact Kristie Schlauraff and Kate Kasten-Mutkus with questions at kristie.schlauraff@stonybrook.edu.

items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.excerpt: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. items.fullDescription: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a text. In Dreaming by the Book , Elaine Scarry describes the function of poetry and novels as "instructions for mental composition" (244). That is, a text encourages readers to fill in the blanks; to reconstruct for themselves certain sensations, emotions, etc. These blanks, according to Wolfgang Iser in The Implied Reader , require readers to draw upon imagination, whereby meaning is created. Ultimately, literature encourages us to envision realities and modalities outside of our own. It is for this reason that reading fiction is considered to be an exercise in empathy--which Marco Caracciolo and Karin Kukkonen conceptualize to be a form of feeling with; of "imagining what we take him or her to be experiencing at a given moment" ( With Bodies: Narrative Theory and Embodied Cognition , 76). This seminar invites papers which attend to the function of visualization, imagination, and/or empathy in reading. In particular, participants are asked to consider how texts across a variety of genres, languages, time periods, cultural contexts, and subject positions, encourage similar or convergent ways of visualization, imagination, and empathy. Can we say reading is "thinking in images"? To what degree do texts encourage the generation of mental imagery and does this necessarily lead us to empathize? How does reading differ phenomenologically from engagement with other arts and mediums? What are the implications of cultivating an embodied and empathetic reading experience, particularly in an era of increasing polarization and automatization? How do certain texts reflect historical and cultural variations in bodily experience? We welcome interdisciplinary approaches drawing from affect theory, narratology, reader-response theory, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cognitive literary studies, and other related fields. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Theories of mind (ToM) and cognitive approaches to reading; embodied models of reading. The impact of genre and form(at): fiction vs. non-fiction, literary vs. genre fiction, nonstandard/"non-literary" texts. Differences across bodies: gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, and/or ability of readers, authors, narrators, and/or characters. Reading in translation or in different languages and effects on the ways we visualize, imagine, and empathize. Theories of imagination, literary imagination, and limits to imagination in reading. Narratological inquiries; impact of perspective and focalization impact on how we visualize and empathize. Reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence. How do AI/LLMs read and how do we read works produced by them?

items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? items.fullDescription: Jordan Peele's Us is a critically acclaimed horror original about government-manufactured clones that are forced to mimic the lives of the people who live on the surface like stringless puppets. While Peele focuses more on a physical tethering, there is a psychological tethering that can be gleamed from this piece, specifically as it relates to the idea of double consciousness. In his work "The Striving of the Negro People," W.E.B. Du Bois describes this idea as "this sense of always looking at oneself through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt or pity. One ever feels his two-ness-an American, a Negro, two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder." These "warring ideas" can exist in any group as the numerous stereotypes, prejudices, and misconceptions alive and well in the world has convinced many to fashion a Franksteined-version of themselves in the hopes of being accepted or safe. The jerky, uncoordinated movements of the tethered from the movie are the perfect metaphor for this forced reality. People attempting to push themselves to live in ways they were not meant to and should not have to. This panel is asking participants to provide submissions that explore the many ways this "tethering" has manifested in the world and explain the impact had on people's lives or how this knowledge can be used as a way to empower people and bring communities together. In other words, in what ways could we be tethered to unfair or unjust interpretations in the world and/or how could our lived experiences be used to untether us from opinions and views that do not empower us and help us build healthy communities? The chair welcomes essays, critical analysis, creative non-fiction, hybrid works, and excerpts of longer pieces.

items.fullDescription: In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us-to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience "somewhere else," (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it. However, the veil is lifting, and "somewhere else" has reached us directly--worker and labor exploitation, droughts and systemic extermination of wild animals, widening class gaps, heat waves, short and snowless winters, floods, wildfires, unprecedented weather patterns, booming microbe populations that alter the very soil we stand on. A sustainable future must be an inconvenient one, and perhaps a precarious one, unless we can remake communities with a focus on outmoded forms of convenience: reciprocity, mutual aid, de-suburbanization, and anti-capitalism. In this panel, we hope to facilitate a conversation about art, in/convenience, precarity, and resistance in community. We also hope to consider alternate views of in/convenience: What can we do to create communities in which the inconvenience of slowness is celebrated rather than derided? How can we utilize writing to grieve futures that didn't materialize? How might we create work that celebrates the pleasure of systemic and interpersonal inconvenience? How can we build resilience to inconvenience and precarity at once, together? In the tradition of scholars and writers like Lauren Berlant, Hanif Abdurraqib, Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing, and Margaret Price, how can we embrace the inconvenient as a site of connection and resistance? We welcome writers of creative nonfiction, poetry, fiction, art pieces, and hybrid works who seek to consider community and in/convenience. items.fullDescription: This panel explores how contemporary and classic crime narratives shift the locus of detection from the isolated individual to distributed, relational, and community-based forms of knowledge. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we examine how detective fiction increasingly foregrounds collective intelligence, local knowledge, and alternative epistemologies as central to the process of solving crime. Moving beyond the figure of the singular, authoritative detective, these texts highlight networks of care, memory, and perception-elderly women whose knowledge is rooted in community history, neurodivergent investigators whose cognitive difference enables pattern recognition outside normative frameworks, and collaborative or participatory forms of detection emerging across media, including television, podcasts, and digital platforms. In these cases, detection becomes less an act of control and more a process of relational engagement and shared sense-making. This panel also considers the role of more-than-human agents in reshaping the boundaries of detection. From artificial intelligences to hybrid or reluctant observers, such figures complicate traditional notions of authority, agency, and responsibility, raising questions about what it means to know and who-or what-can participate in that knowing. By reframing crime fiction as a site of distributed cognition and communal problem-solving, this panel argues that the genre offers a powerful framework for understanding how communities generate knowledge, negotiate truth, and enact forms of justice outside hierarchical or authoritarian models. We invite papers that examine detection as an emergent, collective process and that explore how narrative forms across literature, film, television, games, and podcasts contribute to new imaginaries of empowerment and agency. Possible Topics• Collective detection in true crime podcasts • Fan communities and participatory investigation • Distributed intelligence in television ensembles • Elderly women as custodians of community knowledge • Neurodivergence as alternative epistemology • AI and more-than-human detectives • Detection as care, repair, and relational ethics • Global and decolonial community-based justice systems • Games and interactive detection

The female body evolves from a passive object of desire into an active, expressive, and economically productive site. Thus, women transform spaces of suppression to places of resistance and empowerment. Hussain et al. (2025) note that emancipation precedes autonomy and decision-making in socio-economic spheres. items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. items.fullDescription: This panel examines academic freedom not only as an individual right, but as a collective condition necessary for the production, circulation, and contestation of knowledge within democratic societies. In alignment with the theme of Empowering Communities, we consider how academic freedom enables communities-within and beyond the university-to participate in processes of inquiry, critique, and meaning-making. The panel is structured around three interconnected vantage points. First, it addresses academic freedom as a legal and institutional framework, tracing its historical development and examining contemporary challenges, including policy restrictions, political pressures, and shifts in governance. Second, it considers the classroom as a site where academic freedom is enacted, negotiated, and sometimes constrained, focusing on pedagogical practices that foster open dialogue, critical engagement, and the capacity to navigate disagreement. Third, it explores the future of academic freedom in a changing political and technological landscape, asking how institutions, educators, and communities might work to sustain and rebuild conditions for intellectual autonomy and democratic participation. Across these perspectives, the panel foregrounds the role of academic freedom in supporting not only scholarly inquiry, but also broader forms of social engagement and collective agency. Participants are invited to consider how academic freedom can be understood as a shared responsibility and an evolving practice, rather than a static or purely individual entitlement. Possible Topics• Academic freedom and democratic institutions • Legislative and policy challenges to higher education • The classroom as a space of risk, dialogue, and dissent • Student voice, participation, and vulnerability • Pedagogies of disagreement and difficult conversations • Academic labor, precarity, and speech constraints • Institutional governance and autonomy • Rebuilding trust in higher education • Academic freedom in digital and platformed environments • Global perspectives on academic freedom

This roundtable will explore innovation and empowerment in the language classroom and in language learning communities, where culture is the key to empowerment and innovation. We will reflect on new ways for creating community, creating spaces of innovation, and connecting the classroom to the larger world outside the classroom and to the university through culture and collective action. We welcome presentations that showcase novel pedagogical ideas, lived experiences, and creative practices in language teaching and cultural engagement.

items.fullDescription: Thomas Mann, who would have been 100 in 2025, left readers a number of critical challenges. For one, the coded way in which Mann writes about his most dangerous subjects (homosexuality; knowledge of German guilt) still can fool by a credulous reader, meanwhile his essentializing treatment of race, gender, ethnicity, and class is shockingly unabashed. Then, there is the problem of Mann's reversal of political attitudes as the Nazis drove him-the loyalest of native sons-from Germany. As a young reactionary during the First World War, Mann wrote Reflection of an Unpolitical Man, showing such sympathy with the German politics of expansion and aggression in it that he famously considers whether perhaps the sinking of the Lusitania was a reasonable price to pay for the special German destiny. In the aftermath of World War II, under pressure from his children, Mann publicly denounced the Third Reich. Today, he is widely celebrated as a champion of democracy and opponent of Nazism on the global stage. This panel invites responses to the many contradictions of Mann's personality, which permeate his novels, diaries, and essays with remarkable consistency. Responses need not attempt to resolve these discrepancies, but rather interpret them. How do you relate to Mann as an authorial figure? Are there works by him you find troubling but love anyway? This is an opportunity to practice approaching an author's style with sympathetic care and moral scrutiny in equal part. In addition to Mann's queerness and biraciality (both of which he handled with discomfiting ambivalence), topics mights include such Thomas Mann favorites as music, medicine, language, philosophy, and even cinematography. Comparisons with other authors, artists, and theorists also welcome.

items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]': BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a "special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States" in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this 'special relationship' has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years. The 2026 BAAS Postgraduate Symposium invites proposals from postgraduate researchers at all levels and across all disciplines on the topic of Transatlantic Connections and the 'Special Relationship[s]'. By using the term 'Special Relationship[s]', we intend to explore the relationship between not only the US and the UK, but also between the US and other countries. We invite panels and individual papers on this theme and encourage you to interpret it as broadly as you wish, including any aspect of the US's transnational cultural, political and literary connections, influences or contrasts. We welcome contributions from all realms of American Studies, including, but not limited to: literature and film studies, postcolonial and decolonial analysis, science and visual culture, and urban and environmental history. As this year's symposium will be held at V&A East Storehouse, the site of the David Bowie Archive, we are particularly keen on hearing from scholars exploring the etymologically and culturally rich prefix of the term 'Transatlantic' itself. This one-day symposium will involve not only academic panel discussions, but other activities such as a career development session, an introduction to the archives at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and a keynote address by Professor Mark Ford. The intention is to foster a strong postgraduate community in American Studies and to learn from both our peers and from leaders in our field. The symposium will be catered, hosted primarily in-person at V&A East Storehouse, but with a digital attendance option for those only able to join online. There will be time in the day to explore V&A East Storehouse and the David Bowie Centre. V&A East Storehouse is a working museum store with a rich archive for students to use in their research. The building is designed to allow visitors to get closer to objects held in the V&A collections and to the work of the museum itself. We welcome the submission of individual papers as well as proposals for complete panels of three researchers. Applications from groups of three or four researchers for roundtable discussions are also welcome. For panel and roundtable proposals, please also include a statement of up to 200 words on the aims of the collective submission, alongside the individual papers. Papers should be around 15-20 minutes long , and roundtables will consist of five-minute introductions by each researcher followed by 45 minutes of discussion. Interdisciplinary paper, panel and roundtable proposals are encouraged. Suggested paper and roundtable topics include, but are not limited to: - Case studies or broader comparisons between literary texts from the US and other nations - Case studies or broader comparisons between films from the US and other nations - Comparative political or historical analyses concerning the US and other nations - Comparative economic, scientific or environmental analyses concerning the US and other nations. Although the symposium will centre on 'Transatlantic Connections', we welcome proposals making any transnational comparisons rooted in American Studies. We especially encourage researchers from across Europe and beyond to submit and attend, as part of ongoing efforts to expand the EAAS community of postgraduates. items.fullDescription: REMINDER: SEPTEMBER 22 SUBMISSION DEADLINE American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102.
