items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.excerpt: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. items.fullDescription: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the exception but the rule," as Walter Benjamin theorized. It is not a single event but what Lauren Berlant called a norm "embedded" in the everyday. In the zones of crisis and in daily life, the emergency overwhelms the senses, requiring constant self-governance and limiting our political imagination. The urgent threat of climate change, though often disavowed, is at the center of today's general atmosphere of crisis. Walls hold back displaced populations and rising seas. Earth systems sustain lasting damage. Species are devastated. And with apocalyptic alacrity, capitalist-imperialist competition crosses terrains that were once uninviting and hostile, from deserts to the polar regions and outer space. So far, discourses of risk and emergency have mostly been a boon for the racist right and anti-democratic technocrats, rather than contributing to a genuine project of planetary stewardship. The quest for "energy sovereignty" has unleashed a wave of extractive interventions in the Global South amid the collapse of the postwar international order, creating new sacrifice zones and colonial resource frontiers. Amid widespread doubts about electoral institutions' ability to deliver systemic transformation, some environmentalists have even embraced climate doomerism or the technosolutionism of geoengineering. We see how climate crisis is increasingly governed through biopolitical management, securitized borders, and technocratic forms of environmental control-and how the emergency becomes yet another opportunity for further administration. Crisis discourse often privileges spectacular catastrophe while obscuring the slow, uneven, and racialized forms of ecological violence embedded in everyday life. Unlike the "fevered immediacy that governs the society of the catastrophe-as-spectacle," as Rob Nixon writes, unspectacular "slow violence" is dispersed over time. With the sirens blaring, it is easy to lose sight of the material impacts of the ideology of crisis across time and space. We can also miss the ways in which the permanent emergency warps our cultural production and social relations, concealing the most pressing contradictions of capitalism today. How might we map the cartography of crisis? In doing so, might we open space for alternative ways of thinking and living within and against crisis? How do we hold crisis at bay long enough to bring about a "real state of emergency," as Benjamin says is our task? Jason W. Moore (Binghamton) and Gökçe Günel (Rice) will deliver keynote addresses at the conference, which will also feature a curated program of poetry readings and film screenings. In Case of Emergency is organized by Aditi Kini, Tadhg Larabee, Ernest Lee, and Yolian Ogbu in collaboration with the Chicago Center for Contemporary Theory, and with support from the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization. To apply, submit an abstract (max. 300 words) and a CV via this Google form by June 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Fj4r9oAk5r8b6Q5K6 We want to investigate how crisis is produced, circulated, and inhabited across domains, including climate, culture, political economy, media, and governance. Through this cartography of crisis, we hope to understand how we might countermap and counteract this state of ecological and social emergency. We invite proposals from graduate students in the humanities and social sciences, as well as artists, writers, and other practitioners. Our goal is to create space for imagination and speculation with people of varied backgrounds, interests, and praxes. We welcome interdisciplinary scholarship and cultural criticism attentive to the cultural, aesthetic, historical, and political dimensions of crisis. We imagine submissions might discuss: Technosolutionism and the dilemmas of growth Speculation, commodities, and disaster capitalism Fossil life as economy and desire Green neoliberalism as a political and cultural form Enclosure and destruction of the commons: water, forests, air and more Hydrocolonialism, oceanic crisis, and blue humanities Border ecologies, displacement, and the production of space State-making, world-making, and the remaking of political, social and ecological orders Toxic temporalities, slow violence, and "post"-colonial precarity Apocalypse and new worlds in literature and culture Climate pessimisms and the politics of fear and hope in crisis Resistance, strikes, and land back: movements and solidarity Community, care, and affective ecologies of crisis Participants without access to institutional funding will have the opportunity to request travel support, though we cannot guarantee it. Questions for the organizers can be sent to ccct@uchicago.edu.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Geographies of Horror Department of English Studies (University of Zadar) in collaboration with The Society for the Study of the American Gothic (SSAG) Keynote speaker: Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University) May 20-21st 2027, University of Zadar (Zadar, Croatia) The study of horror has always been inseparable from the question of space. From the shadowed corridors of Gothic castles to contemporary digital voids, spaces in horror are never just passive backdrops. They function as active agents that shape perception, destabilize subjectivity, and collapse the distinction between interior and exterior, revealing how fragile our sense of spatial coherence can be. This conference seeks to understand how spaces become haunted - materially, symbolically, psychologically, and technologically, and how these hauntings articulate broader cultural anxieties, historical traumas, and epistemological uncertainties. In Gothic and horror traditions, fear unfolds through space, guiding perception, and encounters with the unknown. Early Gothic forms, such as castles and monasteries, establish models of spatial excess, enclosure, and architectural anxiety, while the haunted house transforms domestic familiarity into something uncanny. In modern and contemporary horror, this logic extends to urban environments, where entire cities and infrastructures become haunted. While urban legends and other unsettling narratives embed fear in everyday life, abandoned malls, transit systems, and brutalist structures evoke concepts such as "non-places," characterized by transience and anonymity. At the same time, horror increasingly stages the breakdown of spatial logic itself. Non-Euclidean geometries, infinite corridors, and paradoxical environments destabilize perception and challenge epistemological certainty. In these instances, space becomes fundamentally unknowable, aligning with cosmic horror and philosophical pessimism. These concerns extend into digital and virtual environments, where video games, online narratives, and immersive technologies generate new forms of spatial horror. Phenomena such as The Backrooms exemplify liminal, endlessly reproducible environments that evoke both familiarity and existential dread. Simultaneously, haunted space becomes internalized within the body and mind, as psychological and body horror depict interiority as fragmented and invasive. With all this in mind, we welcome papers from across disciplines and media that examine the spatial dimensions of horror, including but not limited to: Gothic and classical haunted spaces Urban and infrastructural hauntings, including "non-places" Non-Euclidean, paradoxical, and incoherent spatialities Digital and virtual environments (games, online narratives, immersive media) The body and subjectivity as haunted spaces Ecological and environmental horror Spatial storytelling across literature, film, television, comics, and interactive media The keynote speaker for the event will be Professor Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock (Central Michigan University). He is a Professor of English at Central Michigan University, where he teaches a range of courses on American literature and popular culture. He is the founder and president of The Society for the Study of the American Gothic, the founder and general editor of the peer-reviewed journal American Gothic Studies, and the co-founder and past chair of the Modern Language Association Gothic Studies Forum. He also serves as the associate editor in charge of horror for the Los Angeles Review of Books and is currently the general editor for Bloomsbury Publishing's six-volume Cultural History of Monsters series. His research focuses on the "cultural work" performed by the Gothic in its various manifestations - the ways in which Gothic texts and practices give shape to culturally specific anxieties and desires. This interest has led him from considering, for example, how nineteenth-and early twentieth-century American women made use of Gothic conventions as a strategy to express discontentment with their circumscribed roles to thinking about the ways contemporary monsters reflect shifting American fears and aspirations. To date, he is the author or editor of 34 books and more than 100 essays and book chapters on the Gothic, American literature, cult film, and popular culture. Abstracts of 250-300 words, accompanied by a short bio (approximately 100 words) and 3-5 keywords, should be submitted to geographyhorror@gmail.com . The deadline for the abstract submission is October 1st 2026. Selected papers focused on American Gothic and horror themes will also be considered for publication in the American Gothic Studies Journal.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PRESENTATION PAPER ABSTRACTS "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" Students, researchers, faculty members, and scholars working in sociology and related social sciences are invited to submit conference presentation paper abstracts for an open conference session entitled "Are Karl Marx's 'Perpetuum Mobile' and/or Max Weber's 'Machine State' Dominating Labor Today? Why or Why Not?" The session will be part of the XXI International Sociological Association (ISA) World Congress of Sociology, from July 4-10, 2027, at Chonnam National University in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City, Korea. Karl Marx and Max Weber both thought about a time when machines would dominate labor. Marx wrote of a "perpetuum mobile" to describe the unceasing turnover of money by a machine of indestructible materiality, circulating a repeating and alternating flow of sale and purchase. Max Weber's "Sociology of Domination" theory warned that the power to coerce markets endlessly would cause endless conflicts. For Marx social change entailed communist revolution, while Weber, who was not a Marxist, worried that social change would be constricted to political coups to control the government's informational infrastructure. Social problems of alienation and rationalization, capitalist wealth and inequality, abuse of power and authority, coerced markets, money hording and social stratification are as alive today as when Marx and Weber set down theories about these social problems over a hundred years ago. What can we say about our AI dominated world using the concepts and writings of Marx and Weber today? Do their economic and historical comparative concepts help us understand our digital world? Why or why not? Submit presentation abstracts by October 14, 2026, through the ISA Congress Submission System link below. items.fullDescription: Since the widespread emergence of Generative AI a few years ago, educators across disciplines have been reconsidering how technology shapes teaching, learning, writing, and assessment. While some departments and faculty have leaned into these new Large Language Models and the technological "advances" they offer, others have worked just as diligently to keep AI out of their classrooms. In light of the recent ban on GenAI in K-8 classrooms by New York City Public Schools, it is possible that the tides in education are going to shift away from AI and back to the uniquely human approach to education. As institutions and educators continue to debate the role of GenAI in education, questions about how to teach effectively without these technologies have become increasingly important. I am currently seeking contributions from interdisciplinary teachers and scholars for a proposed collection on "Teaching without GenAI in the Age of AI." This volume aims to explore pedagogical strategies for instructing without AI. While recent publications look at how to incorporate AI into writing instruction or discuss the complicated nuances of AI in writing classrooms, there is a gap in the field regarding practical approaches on how to instruct without AI in the classroom. Questions to consider include: - How have you structured assignments to prevent AI from being used? - How has your discipline been affected by AI, and how have you worked to keep it out of your classroom? - What pedagogical, disciplinary, ethical, or learning goals motivate your decision to teach without generative AI? - What are your success stories, or failures, of teaching without AI? - How are your students responding to work without AI? - What policies, structures, or pedagogical practices have you used to discourage or prohibit unauthorized AI use? - Have you faced disciplinary contexts that make AI counterproductive? - What role does technology now play in your classroom? - Have you designed any pedagogical experiments or studies to assess your students' learning within a no-AI context? I invite contributions from teachers and scholars across disciplines and educational contexts, including K-12, higher education, and professional education. I am particularly interested in contributions that offer concrete strategies and resources for other educators to implement in their classrooms. Because this volume is intended to be a practical resource as well as a scholarly contribution, submissions that provide example assignments, lesson plans, classroom policies, assessment strategies, or other teaching materials are especially welcome. In order to make this resource available in a timely fashion and respond to existing publisher interest, please send an abstract of no more than 500 words and a brief biographical statement by October 15, 2026 to teachingwithoutgenai@gmail.com. Completed essays will be approximately 4,000 - 5,000 words and will be due by January 31, 2027.

items.fullDescription: Call For Paper Women And Art: Representation, Creativity, And Resistance Open Access | Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, Germany Edited by Habib Tekin & Ay?enur Özkan I??k Art has long served as a powerful space in which gender identities, social roles, cultural expectations, and forms of resistance are constructed, questioned, and reimagined. Across different historical periods and cultural contexts, women have participated in artistic production as creators, performers, patrons, critics, and subjects of representation. Yet their contributions have frequently been shaped by unequal access to artistic institutions, dominant aesthetic traditions, and gendered structures of visibility and recognition. The conference "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance" invites scholars, researchers, artists, and postgraduate students to explore the complex and changing relationship between women and artistic production. The conference seeks to bring together interdisciplinary perspectives on how women create, experience, interpret, and transform art, as well as how femininity and gender are represented within different artistic forms. We particularly welcome contributions that examine the ways in which art can function as a space of memory, identity formation, cultural negotiation, political intervention, and resistance. Papers may address historical or contemporary contexts and may focus on individual artists, artistic movements, particular works, comparative perspectives, or broader theoretical questions concerning women, gender, and aesthetics. The proposed book seeks to examine the representation, production, and experience of women in art from gendered, cultural, and interdisciplinary perspectives, including but not limited to the following areas: Women artists in historical and contemporary contexts Representations of women in art Women and literature Women in painting, sculpture, and visual arts Women in photography and film Women in theatre, performance, dance, and music Feminist art and feminist aesthetics Gender and artistic representation The female body in art Self-representation and female subjectivity Women, creativity, and authorship Women and artistic institutions Gender inequality and exclusion in the art world Women artists and cultural memory Art, trauma, testimony, and memory Women, war, migration, exile, and displacement Art and resistance Women and political art Women and censorship Queer and intersectional approaches to women and art Race, ethnicity, class, and gender in artistic production Postcolonial and decolonial approaches to women and art Women and indigenous artistic traditions Women and popular culture Digital art, social media, and new forms of female creativity Artificial intelligence, technology, and women in art Women as patrons, collectors, curators, and critics Gendered spaces and artistic production Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches to women and art The book particularly encourages contributions that offer close readings of literary works, films, visual artworks, photography, theatre, performance, music, digital media, or other artistic forms, as well as theoretically grounded analyses that advance current debates on women, gender, and art. We look forward to receiving proposals that critically engage with the intersections of women, creativity, representation, identity, memory, and resistance across artistic and cultural contexts and contribute to ongoing scholarly discussions within Gender Studies, Art Studies, Cultural Studies, Literary Studies, and related fields. Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 200-250 words with 5 keywords. A short biographical note (not more than 150 words), including institutional affiliation and key publications. Please include full contact details. The subject line of the email should state: Submission of Abstracts for the Edited Volume on "Women and Art: Representation, Creativity, and Resistance." Authors selected for inclusion will be invited to submit full chapters (approximately 6,000-7,000 words, including references) following acceptance of the proposal by the publisher. Abstract Submission Deadline: 15 October 2026 Full-Text Submission Deadline: 15 February 2027 Eligibility Contributors are required to hold a PhD. Alternatively, submissions may be co-authored, provided that at least one co-author holds a PhD. In addition, PhD candidates are welcome to submit contributions within their own field of research, particularly if the proposed chapter is directly related to their doctoral project and falls within the thematic and conceptual parameters of this book. Publisher The volume will be published by Maurer Press, Frankfurt am Main, an established publishing house with 35 years of publishing experience. Publication Fee The publication fee for accepted contributions is 115€. Abstracts and inquiries should be sent to: women.art.literature@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Edited volume proposed for Manchester University Press's French Film Directors series I am seeking two additional contributors for an edited volume devoted to the work of French filmmaker Nicole Garcia, currently in preparation for submission to Manchester University Press's French Film Directors series. The series editors have already expressed strong interest in the project. Although Garcia has established one of the most distinctive bodies of work in contemporary French cinema-spanning more than three decades and including films such as Place Vendôme (1998), L'Adversaire (2002), Selon Charlie (2006), Un balcon sur la mer (2010), Mal de pierres (2016), and Amants (2020)-her work as a director has received relatively little sustained scholarly attention in either French or English. This volume aims to provide the first comprehensive critical study of Garcia's filmmaking, bringing together scholars from film studies and related disciplines to explore the aesthetic, narrative, thematic, cultural, and institutional dimensions of her work. The project seeks to examine Garcia's cinema through a range of critical and methodological perspectives, combining close analyses of individual films with broader discussions of the contexts in which her work has been produced and received. Contributions informed by interdisciplinary approaches are particularly welcome. Possible areas of inquiry Proposals may address, but are not limited to, the following topics: -Aesthetic and formal strategies: mise-en-scène, spatial construction, narrative ellipsis, secrecy, and revelation. -Genre and narrative form: melodrama, romantic narratives, psychological drama, and narrative complexity. -Adaptation and screenwriting: literary adaptation, intermediality, and processes of cinematic creation. -Gender and subjectivity: female desire, intimacy, ambivalence, vulnerability, and representations of femininity. -Performance and authorship: Garcia's trajectory from actress to filmmaker, her direction of actors, and her engagement with stardom. -Social relations and identities: masculinity, class, family relationships, and bourgeois social worlds. -Memory and temporality: nostalgia, personal and collective memory, displacement, and the relationship between past and present. -Industrial and institutional contexts: production and funding structures, festival circulation, and the position of women directors within the French film industry. -Comparative and interdisciplinary approaches: connections with other filmmakers, European art cinema, literature, gender studies, memory studies, cultural studies, and related fields. Contributors are welcome to focus on one or more individual films, provided their analyses engage with the broader concerns of the volume. Comparative approaches are also encouraged, with Garcia's directorial work remaining central to the discussion. The volume seeks not only to foreground Garcia's contribution as a filmmaker but also to use her work as a lens through which to explore broader questions of authorship, gender, cinematic form, and the cultural economy of contemporary French cinema. Submission guidelines The volume is expected to comprise approximately 10-12 chapters of 6,000-7,000 words each. Prospective contributors are invited to submit an abstract of approximately 500 words, clearly outlining the proposed chapter's central argument, theoretical or methodological framework, and the specific aspects of Garcia's cinema it will examine. Submissions should also include: -Full name and current institutional affiliation; -Contact information; -A short biographical note. Deadline for abstracts: October 15, 2026 Please submit your proposal using the following link: https://www.dropbox.com/request/ykp0stxbqk5dhsjnhl7m The book proposal is scheduled for submission to Manchester University Press in fall 2026. The deadline for completed chapters will be communicated once the publication timetable has been established, and contributors will be given sufficient time to prepare their manuscripts. Scholars at all career stages, including early-career researchers, are warmly encouraged to submit proposals. Editor and contact Dr Romain Chareyron (roc104@usask.ca) Associate Professor of French Department of Languages, Literatures and Cultural Studies University of Saskatchewan, Canada

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTER PROPOSALS Eating for a Green Future: Literature, Culture, and the Politics of Food in Contemporary India Edited by Dr. Manisha Mohanty (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University & Fulbright-Nehru Fellow) Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak (MLA Bibliography Fellow, MLA) Dr. Sonali Das (Assistant Professor, S'O'A University) This edited volume begins from a single premise: food cannot be discussed apart from the politics that surround it. Questions around production and consumption are inseparable from issues of hunger, malnutrition, social inequality, and ecological crisis. The concept of 'food culture', understood as the cooking and eating of food, must be reexamined in the light of sustainability and structural violence. Industrial agriculture, multinational food corporations, and extreme disparities in access have made eating an exercise of power as much as of nourishment. In India, the evidence is stark. Farmer suicides, shrinking biodiversity, corporate-controlled food systems, and climate-induced crop failures expose the systemic inequalities that run through the country's foodways. The volume gathers essays on literature, film, digital media, and everyday food practice, investigating how contemporary texts address climate change, agribusiness, land dispossession, toxic labour, and food scarcity. One question threads through the whole collection: how much of what we eat still comes from traditional, community-based knowledge, and how much is determined by global agribusiness, whose interest lies in maximizing profit rather than social welfare or universal nourishment? This leads us to explore how corporate food systems blur the distinction between inherited culinary practices and their commodified imitations. The result is a food culture in which authenticity itself becomes a marketing strategy. This volume works across food studies, environmental humanities, and popular culture, and its ambition is both practical and critical: to propose justice-oriented frameworks for rethinking consumption, appetite, and sustainability. Proposed Themes: • Food and sustainability: How can food culture foreground sustainability and ecological concerns rather than mere novelty or elitist pleasure? • Culinary knowledge and agribusiness: How much of what we eat today emerges from traditional ecological knowledge, local seed cultures, and community foodways, and what is shaped by agribusiness, multinational food corporations, and algorithmically curated "choices"? • Rethinking consumption: How can we rethink everyday modes of eating, cooking, and appetite to bring about positive ecological change and more equitable food systems? • Power and intersectionality: How does the intersection of food studies and environmental studies illuminate caste, class, and racial hierarchies, gendered labour, and entrenched social inequalities? • Food justice: How do literary texts, films, digital campaigns, and social media food cultures imagine or fail to imagine food justice, and how might these imaginaries inform public policy and activism? Proposed Structure: Part I: Food, Ecology, and Justice · Food politics, food justice, and environmental humanities · Traditional ecological knowledge and culinary/cultural memory · Rethinking appetite and taste in times of climate crisis Part II: Literature, Film, and Visual Culture · Novels and memoirs centred on famine, scarcity, or ecological degradation · Regional food literatures · Films that foreground drought, crop failure, farmer suicides, or agrarian distress Part III: Digital Foodscapes, Social Media, Influencers, and Algorithms · Hashtag activism around hunger, food waste, land rights, and seed sovereignty · Corporate influence in online food marketing · Online recipe cultures as spaces of resistance (low-waste cooking, foraging, veganism, zero-waste influencers, etc.) Part IV: Politics and the Future of Food · Analysing policy texts, food security laws, and welfare schemes through a cultural lens · Grassroots food sovereignty movements, community kitchens, seed banks · Frameworks for sustainable and just food futures grounded in local knowledge systems · Pedagogy: teaching food-environment issues in classrooms, community settings, and online spaces Part V: Special Section India/Odisha · Indigenous and Adivasi food knowledge · Cyclone-prone ecologies and coastal food insecurity · Temple food cultures · Gendered kitchen labour in rural and urban India/Odisha · Caste-based food taboos and community food practices · Land, mining, and displacement affecting food systems Submission Guidelines: We invite scholars, independent researchers, and practitioners working in literary and cultural studies, environmental humanities, food studies, media studies, and related fields to submit original, unpublished chapter proposals. Interdisciplinary and comparative approaches are especially encouraged. Proposals should include: • An abstract of 300-350 words outlining the chapter's argument, methodology, and primary texts or case studies • 5-6 keywords • A short biographical note (75-100 words) with full name, institutional affiliation, and contact details Full chapters should be: • 5,000-8,000 words in length, inclusive of notes and references • Follow MLA style (9th edition) • Original, previously unpublished, and not under review elsewhere Timeline: • Abstract submission deadline: 15 October 2026 • Notification of acceptance: 20 November 2026 • Full chapter submission: 28 February 2027 Submission: Please send abstracts and biographical notes as a single Word document to: Dr. Shashibhusan Nayak: shashienglish@gmail.com and Dr. Manisha Mohanty: manishamohanty@soa.ac.in Publication: Following the review of abstracts and full chapters, the completed manuscript will be submitted to Bloomsbury for consideration. All chapters will undergo peer review as part of the standard editorial and publisher review process.

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "The Human Cost of Migration? Case-Studies From Britain and China," edited by Robert Walker and Rachel Murphy. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 October 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue Internal and international migration are often discussed in different intellectual and political spaces which obscures important common features. Internal (or domestic) migration, typically referring to movement from rural to urban areas, is frequently construed as an important mechanism-sometimes planned, although often not-that facilitates economic development, urbanisation and the more effective utilisation of the factors of production. Equally migration has regularly been blamed for escalating housing costs, causing over-crowding, and resulting in the development of slums and criminality. International migration is simultaneously viewed as a cornerstone of global development, necessary according to the UN International Organization for Migration for the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals 1, 3, 8,10, 13 and 16, while others portray it as 'invasion' and a mechanism of 'civilizational erasure'. While most international migration is economic and legal, governed by work permits and quotas and driven by demand for workers and people's aspirations for career development and a better life, political attention tends to focus on illicit migration, asylum seekers and refugees. Much political discourse is framed from the perspective of host communities establishing rules that limit the right of migrants to enter cities and countries and/or to enjoy services available to natives. Academic research has tended to be disproportionately quantitative focused on stocks, flows and spatial concentrations. Where the aspirations and experiences of migrants have been considered, often they have been dissected into variables that lose connection with the people whose experiences they index. What has frequently been neglected is the story of the migrant experience told from the perspective of migrants themselves. The suspicion is that, examined through this lens, international and domestic migrants share many salient characteristics with respect to motivations, work experience, achievements, challenges, exploitation, humiliation and resilience. It is possible, too, that for some, the costs of migration outweigh the benefits. Therefore, this thematic issue is structured as a natural experiment adopting a maximum difference design. Divided into two sections, the first will contain articles invited to focus on the experience of domestic migrants in China, the second section will comprise articles on the experience of international migrants into the United Kingdom. The editorial will present an analysis of the articles drawing attention to similarities and differences in the experiences of internal and international migrants. It will equally explore the trade-offs that migrants make when seeking to migrate and in accommodating to the place of destination and their success in ensuring that benefits of migration outweigh the costs. Over the last 45 years, China has experienced the largest internal migration in history. This has transformed China from a mostly rural society to an urban one, facilitated unprecedented industrial and commercial growth and China's emergence as the world's second largest economy, and contributed to lifting 800 million people out of extreme poverty. There is evidence, though, that China's economic success has been achieved in part by personal and familial sacrifices made rural-urban migrants that go largely unrecognised in public discourse. Britain, its culture shaped over millennia by waves of inward migration, has nevertheless been transformed into a multicultural society since the 1950s, notably in the last 45 years. In 1951, the foreign-born population comprised 4.3 percent of the total. This proportion was still only 6.6 percent in 1981 but, by 2021, it had risen to 77 percent. In 1951, 99.9 percent of the population was white as was 96 percent in 1981. In marked contrast, by 2021/2 29.4 percent of the population was not white. Although migrants have been largely absorbed into Britian's labour market, sometimes undertaking work shunned by the host population, migration has nevertheless become a toxic political issue. Internal migration intensity has declined over this period despite high mobility for certain age groups. Research articles are invited dealing with the life experiences of (1) internal migrants and their families in China or (2) international migrants and their families into the United Kingdom. There are no constraints on the research methodologies employed provided that they seek to capture the lived experiences of migrants. Articles that discuss the challenges confronted by migrants and report on how migrants maximise the benefits accruing from migration are particularly welcome. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please direct questions to the special issue editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri [edkunkur@mtu.edu] and Dana Van Kooy [drvankoo@mtu.edu] For questions about the use and disclosure of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, please see NANO's AI Statement (https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Journal-Information) Please use the Submission Form on top left of the CFP page: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Submissions/Submission-Form NANO: New American Notes Online is a free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal. NANO does not charge for submission, review, or publication. It is indexed in the MLA International Bibliography, GALE, ProQuest, and DOAJ.

items.fullDescription: Jewish Life between Locality and Mobility Penn Graduate Conference in Jewish Studies, February 28-March 1, 2027 Throughout many periods of their histories, Jews and Jewish communities have developed an ambivalent relationship to the spaces in which they have lived. Jewish collective memory is deeply rooted in the land of Israel, both real and imagined, while simultaneously grounded in a wide array of diasporic localities. From "the wandering Jew" and "the rootless cosmopolitan" to the image of the assimilated Jew, conceptions of Jewishness have been shaped by the contested but strong, ever-evolving ties Jews had to the spaces they inhabited. In modern times, as the Jewish national movement took shape and eventually led to the establishment of the State of Israel, Jews around the world continue to grapple with questions of identity and belonging, safety, resilience, and autonomy in a world where Jewish sovereignty exists alongside longstanding Jewish communities in the diaspora. The Jewish Studies Graduate Conference at the University of Pennsylvania, to be held on the Penn campus in Philadelphia on February 28-March 1, 2027, seeks to explore the relationship between locality and mobility in Jewish life across historical periods and geographical spaces. This interdisciplinary conference will serve as a forum for graduate students to share their research, receive feedback from Penn faculty and fellow graduate students, and learn about ongoing work in the field from peers around the world. We aim to foster a community of emerging scholars who will help shape the global future of Jewish Studies. We welcome contributions from the wide array of disciplines connected with Jewish Studies, including but not limited to: Ancient History Anthropology Archaeology Architecture Art History Geography History Jewish Languages (Hebrew, Ladino, Yiddish, etc.) Linguistics Literary Studies Media Studies Museum Studies Religious Studies Travel and accommodation: Thanks to the generous support of our sponsors, we are able to provide presenters with up to two nights of accommodation in Philadelphia. Limited funds are also available for presenters from outside the Philadelphia area to help defray the cost of travel (economy fare) to and from the conference. To apply: Submit your abstract, not to exceed 300 words, via this link: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdWszlWuD3IeBHGzQgikSNqOTvTaIfZpEI5kcv988WIw6JVlg/viewform?usp=header by October 30. When submitting your abstract, you will also be prompted to indicate whether you would like to apply for a travel grant. Abstracts will be considered independently of this information. This conference is generously sponsored by the Julie Beren Platt and Marc E. Platt Program Fund in Jewish Studies at the University of Pennsylvania.

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The Taylor Swift & Swiftie Studies area invites paper proposals on topics related to Taylor Swift and/or Swifties from multiple vantage points. Since her debut in 2006, Taylor Swift has become a fixture of popular culture. Her career has been marked by incredible record-breaking highs and infamous tabloid-fodder lows. Known for her sharp lyrics, her evolving cross-genre musical styles, and her dedicated, creative fanbase (the Swifties), Swift's influence has been noted within music, fashion, economics, politics, and other cultural spheres of power. As an interdisciplinary area, we invite papers from multiple perspectives and disciplines. Topics might include, but are not limited to: • Critical interpretations of Swift's lyrics, eras, and/or personas • Considerations of Taylor Swift and politics, feminisms, activism and social justice • Interrogations of Swift and gender, race, class, and other identities/identifications • Analyses of Swift's connections to business, law, psychology, philosophy or other academic disciplines • Arguments about fandom, belonging, relating, creating and other Swiftie concerns • Examples of Taylor Swift's pedagogical relevancy All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Taylor Swift and Swiftie Studies area, please contact its Area Chair, Juliette Holder at jholder1@csustan.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR CHAPTERS The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature Editors: Mariusz Finkielsztein (University of Gdan?sk) mariusz.finkielsztein@gmail.com Josefa Ros Velasco (Complutense University of Madrid) josros@ucm.es The Handbook of Boredom in Modern Literature is to be a comprehensive monographic study examining boredom as a central aesthetic, philosophical, psychological, and socio-cultural category in the history of modern literature. Rather than relying purely on abstract theory, this volume approaches boredom through focused case studies devoted to individual authors and their works. Across these chapters, boredom-alongside adjacent states such as ennui, tedium, spleen, acedia, melancholy, existential malaise, and affective exhaustion-emerges variously as paralysis, protest, privilege, illness, and spiritual crisis. By situating close textual readings within the broader intellectual history of modernity, the volume, written by a multidisciplinary group of authors, is to demonstrate that literary boredom is a powerful diagnostic lens on social order, temporality, and the modern subject's experience of meaninglessness. Volume Structure & Epochal Scope The volume is planned as a Handbook or Companion and covers not only the most vital writers addressing the theme of boredom but also a broad selection of modern authors (around 60 chapters). The book is to trace the evolution of literary boredom across (tentatively) seven historical and thematic phases: Early Modernity & Enlightenment Foundations: Early reflections on existential void and social routine (e.g. Diderot, Laclos, Austen). Romantic Ennui (1770s-1840s): Melancholy, idealist frustration, and the world-weary anti-hero (e.g., Goethe, de Stae?l, Senancour, Byron, Chateaubriand, Constant, Stendhal, Sand, Balzac, Musset). The Superfluous Man: The Russian literary archetype of social paralysis, alienation, and unfulfilled potential (e.g. Pushkin, Lermontov, Goncharov, Turgenev). Bourgeois Boredom, Realism, & Decadent Spleen: Domestic stagnation, industrial monotony, social entrapment, and aesthetic decay (e.g., Dickens, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Fontane, Chopin, Ibsen, Gilman, Conrad, Chekhov, Baudelaire, Huysmans, Wilde). Modernist Stagnation (Early 20th C.): Temporal distortion, consciousness, alienation, and metaphysical paralysis (e.g., Proust, Joyce, Pessoa, Mann, Kafka, Woolf). Catastrophism & Existential Absurdity (Mid-20th C.): Totalitarian dread, the absurdity of existence, and postwar existential malaise (e.g., Broch, Platonov, Orwell, H. Miller, Gombrowicz, Sartre, Camus, Beckett, Buzzati, Gracq). Postwar Emptiness, Consumerism, & Digital Fatigue: Mass society, late-capitalist hyper-consumption, information overload, and contemporary affective exhaustion (e.g., Moravia, Perec, de Beauvoir, Ernaux, Bellow, Bernhard, Duras, DeLillo, Houellebecq, Ferrante, Rourke, Moshfegh). Chapter Guidelines & Scope Each chapter must offer an in-depth analysis of the theme of broadly understood boredom in the work of a single author (according to a formula: Boredom in...). The title should include the name and surname of a writer as a main part, and a freely formulated subtitle. Analytical Approach: Authors may focus on a single representative work but should analyse boredom across multiple texts of an author to demonstrate how boredom functions as a recurring motif in the author's oeuvre. Target Audience: Written primarily for readers seeking to deepen their understanding of boredom in a specific author's work (spoilers are permitted), while remaining accessible to a general literary audience. Comparative analysis with other writers should be kept to a minimum. Required Contextual Elements: o Biographical Context: Key details situating the writer within their epoch. Where applicable, personal engagement with boredom (e.g., excerpts from letters, diaries) may be included. o Socio-Cultural Context: Historical background necessary to understand the specific societal structures depicting boredom (e.g., aristocratic class dynamics, marital systems, late-capitalist work environments, author's country history and socio-cultural context). Submission guidelines: The abstract of the proposed chapter (between 250-500 words) along with a short bio (up to 150 words) and contact information should be sent to editors via e-mail before the end of October 2026. Contributors may propose up to two chapters. Each submission must include a brief statement detailing: (a) how the chosen author's work relates to boredom; and (b) what the contributor's expertise is on the writer. The minimum criteria for inclusion of a writer are: the author must address themes of boredom/ennui, possess at least some international recognition, and be available in English translation. Poetry is excluded. The comments and decisions on the proposed chapters will be provided before the end of December 2026. Then, the proposal for the book will be sent to prospective publishers (Routledge Handbook Series, The Oxford Handbooks, The Cambridge Companions or The Palgrave Handbooks). In case of a positive answer from a publisher, the authors will be asked to prepare the chapter, between 6,000 and 8,000 words including footnotes and references. Technical information will be provided after the publisher accepts the proposal and will depend on the publisher's style. In case of any doubts and/or questions, we encourage prospective authors to consult the editors directly. Prospective deadline for chapters: mid-2028

items.fullDescription: John Steinbeck once remarked that fellow-Californian Robinson Jeffers wrote some the "greatest poetry since Whitman." Steinbeck kept a significant collection of Jeffers work both in his personal library and Ed Ricketts' Lab, where Jeffers was an influential topic in their endlessly varied conversations. When asked about possibility of meeting the poet, Steinbeck declined with a telling degree of reverence: "His poetry is perfect to me, and I don't think one should get the man mixed up with his work." Although they did eventually meet-notably when Steinbeck lived in Monterey in 1944-their relationship was one of distant, though friendly, mutual respect. Although these two writers rarely crossed physical paths, their work maintains a wide concurrence of concern. They both deeply engaged with Californian geography and history; they both emphasized the influence of the natural world upon the individual and society; they both had social circles that revolved around the Monterey Peninsula; they both were interested in psychoanalytical theory; they both were students of classical literature and philosophy; they both experienced extraordinary recognition at the peak of their literary fame (at one point, Jeffers was on the cover of Time magazine); they both were deeply uncomfortable with such a cultural spotlight; they both admonished personal humility in the face of environmental forces. Intersections such as these (and many more) deserve to be explored with more depth and significance. The editorial staff at the Steinbeck Review invites submissions for a special edition, "John Steinbeck and Robinson Jeffers." We are particularly interested in perspectives which put these authors into conversation in productive and even unexpected ways. Although submissions are not required to examine both authors, we strongly suggest that they engage (even if briefly) both Steinbeck and Jeffers. We welcome all critical and theoretical perspectives. Please see the full guide for submissions here and submit your paper to the Steinbeck Review's online submission system, found at www.editorialmanager.com/Steinbeck, no later than October 31, 2026. Decisions will be made by December 1, 2026. Submissions should be accompanied by an abstract and key words.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers - Siren! Magazine Second Issue: Disciplined Bodies, Transgressive Bodies, Transformed Bodies Link to the call: https://penn.manifoldapp.org/page/siren-current-call-for-proposals Bodies are shaped by the worlds we inhabit, the stories we tell about them, and the institutions through which we learn what a body is, what it should look like, how it should behave, and what it is permitted to become. Yet bodies are often treated as merely biological facts: fixed, self-evident, and prior to politics. This distinction matters because once something is understood as natural, the expectations attached to it can begin to appear inevitable. For this issue, we invite work on disciplined, transgressive, and transformed bodies. We are interested in work that reflects on how bodily norms are produced and enforced, what happens when bodies exceed or destabilize those norms, and how bodies are remade through political, social, technological, medical, aesthetic, and cultural processes. The question, then, is not only who tells bodies what to do, but how we come to understand what bodies are for in the first place and how we may challenge the constraints imposed over them. How do medicine, law, media, family, religion, workplaces, markets, states, and digital platforms make particular kinds of bodies appear normal, desirable, healthy, productive, legible, or valuable? What happens when a body does not fit the meaning assigned to it; when it refuses, cannot comply, fails to conform, or becomes something else? We are especially interested in moments when bodily categories begin to break down, when the meanings attached to bodies no longer hold, or become further reinforced and are resisted, and when bodies become sites of contradiction, refusal, negotiation, and possibility. Key terms For the purposes of this issue, we understand the three terms broadly and provisionally: Disciplined bodies are shaped by the norms, institutions, and expectations that surround them. They may be expected to reproduce, perform gender recognizably, be deemed healthy and desirable, remain productive and self-optimizing, regulate themselves, and stay intelligible to others. We welcome work on how these norms are produced, enforced, negotiated, and unevenly distributed. Transgressive bodies make those expectations difficult to sustain. Transgression need not be intentional: a body may refuse, fail, exceed, disrupt, or simply be unable to comply. Nor are particular bodies inherently transgressive; they are often rendered so by institutions and cultural frameworks that mark some forms of embodiment as abnormal, excessive, threatening, or unintelligible. Transformed bodies ask what happens when embodiments become a site of remaking. Bodies may be altered through medicine, technology, disability, transition, reproduction, labor, aging, artistic practice, environmental exposure, or political violence. Transformation may be desired or imposed, liberatory, or coercive. We are interested in what bodies become, what histories they carry, what forms of power shape them, and what futures they make imaginable. We welcome submissions that interpret one of these categories, bring two or more into conversation, question the distinctions between them, or propose other ways of thinking about bodily discipline, transgression, and transformation. Proposals should identify the term that most strongly connects to the submission while noting any significant intersections with the others. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: -Bodily autonomy and reproductive rights -Disability and debility -Gender and sexuality -Race and racialization -Beauty and aesthetic labor -Health, illness, and wellness -Medicine and biomedical technologies -Aging -Death -War and militarization -Sport and physical performance -Embodiment and mediation (digital or otherwise) -Surveillance -Cyborg subjectivities -Body modification -Bodily aesthetics -Migration and borders -Carcerality -Labor and productivity -Environmental harm -Colonialism and its afterlives -Speculative or imagined forms of embodiment Who can submit We welcome work from scholars, students, artists, activists, independent researchers, and public intellectuals working in communication, media studies, feminist studies, cultural studies, disability studies, queer and trans studies, critical race studies, the humanities, and related fields. Submissions are open to contributors at all career stages, but we particularly encourage work from early-career scholars and those whose work may sit outside conventional academic publishing structures. Formats Submissions may be written, visual, audiovisual, audio, or hybrid. We welcome experimental forms alongside conventional scholarly approaches. Across formats, submissions should engage the issue's broader commitments to critical feminist inquiry, transnational solidarity, feminist world-making, and transformative social change. Timeline For full consideration, abstracts are due by October 31, 2026, with decisions made by December 10th. Completed submissions will be due by February 10th, 2027, with a projected publication date in September 2027. Guidelines for proposal types -Paper: Please send the title and a 250-word abstract outlining the argument for a full paper featuring an original contribution. Full papers are long-form (3000-5000 words) analytical essays that connect to the current topic of the issue. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Escalator Paper: Please submit the title and a 150-word abstract for a short analytical piece (500-2000 words). Research escalator papers are works-in-progress on novel ideas related to the issue theme; they will be published as submitted and paired with an expert mentor to develop into a full analytical or empirical work. Please use the APA citation system for references. -Multimedia and Hybrid Submissions: Please submit the title and a 200-250-word description explaining how your piece relates to the current issue's theme. For multimedia works, explain how text and other elements interact. Finished pieces should include a link to a sample. For works in progress, add a brief (up to 100 words) outline of the concept, your process, and the timeline for completion. Experimental submissions are encouraged. Important dates Abstract due: October 31, 2026 Acceptances: December 10, 2026 Final submission: February 10, 2027 Peer-review process and mentorships: February - June 2027 Expected publication date: early September 2027 All proposals should be sent as a .docx or .pdf document, and include a brief bio (up to 150 words) introducing yourself and your background. Please submit proposals to asc-sirenmagazine@asc.upenn.edu, using the subject line "Siren Magazine - Bodies." Direct any questions regarding the call or submission process to the same address.

Call for papers | The Aesthetics of Mythmaking: Narrative, Culture, and Power "We are mythmaking creatures" (Ware 2025); human beings make and reinterpret myths. Mythmaking has remained a living action of the human cultural process since the earliest stage of human history. Myths are not static stories that stay unchanged across time; that is why agency and acts of mythmaking are powerful. Through mythmaking, inherited stories are continually adapted and reinterpreted to reflect changing cultural values and historical circumstances. Consequently, myth also assumes the form of a spectacle and ideology that must be critically examined; it often serves to naturalise or essentialise instances of domination, transforming contingent political agendas into "universal" truths. This call for papers values both the aesthetic brilliance of mythmaking in the arts and popular culture and the rigor critique of its ideological utility as a tool for hegemony. The inherent ambiguity of myth as both a meaning-making tool and a mechanism of control invites further scholarly exploration. We therefore seek to gather diverse perspectives on how these creative processes function across human experience, inviting interdisciplinary submissions that weave together multifaceted theories of myth and mythmaking.?? Even the same myth can be retold in radically different ways. For Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, the reinvented myth of Ozymandias represents a meditation on antiquity and the transience of glory. More than a century later, when Alan Moore rewrote Ozymandias in Watchmen, Shelley's ruined king was transformed into a morally ambiguous antagonist with the ambition to construct a new global saviour myth capable of uniting humanity. Moore's self-fashioned Ozymandias also evokes the myth of Superman, a figure that can be traced to Friedrich Nietzsche's concept (1883) of Übermensch (beyond-human). From Nietzschean philosophical ideal of self-overcoming, the Superman later takes forms in different myths: George Bernard Shaw's play and most famously in Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster's comics, where Superman represents the experiences and aspirations of Jewish immigrant communities before being incorporated into American national mythology during WWII and the Cold War. Superman mythmaking also transcended across the Pacific. In postwar Japan, superhumans like Astro-Boy and Ultraman reconstructed the archetype into social recovery and national renewal in the aftermath of atomic destruction. These examples show that mythmaking reinvents cultural symbols into new stories in response to political realities and collective memory. While myths are traditionally framed as archaic narratives of gods and heroes, modern scholars argue that the act of mythmaking can act as a mobilizing force in society and serves as a political power beyond its presence in art (Citton 2025; Josephson-Storm 2017). A political myth operates as a system of explanation, providing a cryptography through which the disconcerting chaos of contemporary facts is ordered and understood (Girardet 1987; Segal 2020). By offering an imaginary reading of a historical moment, myths restore intelligibility to a fractured world, manifesting in recurring structures like the nostalgia for a Golden Age or the yearning for a providential Saviour. However, this phenomenological reality of worldbuilding parallels Walter D. Mignolo's decolonial critique of "enunciation," where the content of myth is disseminated by the enunciator who ultimately possesses power (2018, 144-145).?? Mythmaking is still an ongoing cultural process without a singular definition. In a way, its study can be viewed as a consequence of the emergence of anthropology, which, during the 19th century, inquired about the concept of myth. This was the work of, for example, E.B. Tylor and J.G. Frazer. Yet, they were not so concerned about the aesthetics of mythmaking, as they viewed it as a form of "primitive knowledge" that was the exact opposite of Western art and science. Across the 20th century, authors as diverse as Bronislaw Malinowski (1922), Ernst Cassirer (1946), Claude Lévi-Strauss (1978), Northrop Frye (1967), Carl Jung (1964), Joseph Campbell (2004), and Mircea Eliade (1954) have suggested a whole range of different and often conflictive definitions for this concept. They actively engaged with the knowledge traditions of anthropology, philosophy, history, comparative literature, and religion studies.? One compelling form of analyzing mythmaking emerged at the intersection of aesthetics, philosophy, politics, and critical theory during the 19th century. Reacting against Enlightenment rationalism, German Romantics and Idealists such as Schiller, Schelling, and Hegel called for a "new mythology" to heal the alienation between humanity and nature while birthing the philosophical myth of absence-the belief that modernity is uniquely "mythless" (Josephson-Storm 2017, 17-21). This tension is central to the work of Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, who, echoing Max Weber, argued that the Enlightenment's "disenchantment of the world" sought to dispel myths through reason, yet ultimately revealed that "enlightenment reverts to mythology" (2016, xviii), as instrumental rationality facilitated the domination of human beings over one another. In this way, inquiring the aesthetics of mythmaking involves a critique of different areas of the socio-cultural construct, reaching the realms of narrative, culture, and power.?? Amidst these diverse intellectual traditions and definitions of mythmaking, this call invites contributions that explore mythmaking as an ongoing process of cultural translation, forms of exercising power, political representation, and artistic (re)creation. We are interested in examining how mythmaking is still continually making, remaking, and mobilising new meanings and identities across historical periods, cultural contexts, and media forms. Proposals for thematic articles in response to this call are welcome, including but not limited to the following topics: ? Mythmaking and memory retelling? ? Superstition, hagiographies, and religion stories?? ? Mythmaking in different culturalforms: films, comics, and music? ? Mythmaking and Nationmaking?? ? Mythmaking as Tools of (De)colonial Discourse?? ? Mythmaking and Identity: theInvention of Tradition and Self-making? ? Mythmaking and Imaginary?? ? Lived experience and Phenomenology of Mythmaking ? The Power of Mythmaking in Social and Political Contexts? ? Mysticism and Poetry? ? Myth and Mythmaking in Literature from Romanticism to Modernism? ? Mythopoesia? ? Women Writers/Poets and Feminist Revisionist Mythmaking? ? The Role of Mythmaking in Visual Arts? ? The Study of Mythography in Modern Culture? ? Mythic ecology? ? Mythmaking, Philosophy, and Science: from myth to reason? ? Mythmaking and Psychology (Jungian Psychology, Psychoanalysis, etc)? items.fullDescription: THE SIXTIES Call for proposals: Papers, Sessions, Panels Popular Culture Association Annual Conference March 24-27, 2027 in Boston, MA The Sixties area of the Popular Culture Association welcomes submissions for papers and presentations on any aspect of popular culture from the era. Topics of interest might include, but are not limited to: Film, television, radio, and other media (underground press, posters, etc.) Analysis of influential books/authors, art/artists, films/filmmakers, etc. New developments in religion and spirituality Psychedelia and its many manifestations The sexual revolution Music and fashion, as cultural expression and/or consumer culture New social arrangements, e.g., communes, back to the land movement 1968 or other significant dates, places, or events, e.g., Freedom Summer, Days of Rage, etc. Countercultural movements, e.g., hippies, Diggers, SDS, Black Panther Party, White Panther Party, etc.Politics and protests of the era, e.g., Civil Rights, Vietnam War, Free Speech Movement, etc. Race and gender issues, e.g., Black Power, women's rights, etc. Media representations of/reactions to any of the above Rock music, the counterculture, or other developments in international/global contexts (i.e. outside the US and UK) The significance of the decade in contemporary society and culture, including ongoing debates and revised perspectives NOTE : This year PCA is trying out a wider shared theme for the conference, on the general subject of "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture" - which obviously connects with many Sixties topics. As part of that theme, presenters are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, technological change, or changing cultural practices. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. ALSO : This year we are also featuring a joint panel between the Sixties area and the Radio, Podcast, and Sound Media area. Possible paper topics are wide open, and could include things like: the FM radio revolution in the U.S. (freeform/progressive formats, changes in FCC policies, etc.); significant radio stations, such as WDIA in Memphis, KSAN in San Francisco, etc.; "pirate radio" in the U.K. (Radio Caroline, etc.) and official responses (the creation of BBC1, etc.); the expansion of stereophonic audio in relation to popular music, psychedelic rock, etc.; the influence of/by particular record labels on pop culture and the counterculture (especially independents such as Motown, Vanguard, ESP, etc.); more recent podcasts or other audio media about the 1960s; any of the above in non-U.S./U.K. contexts; and any other related subjects. If you would like your paper submission to be considered for the shared panel(s), please note that on your abstract or via email to the area chair. DEADLINE FOR SUBMISSIONS: October 31, 2026. For individual papers, please submit a title and 300-word abstract. Be sure to proofread your name, title, and abstract closely as this text will become part of the program should your proposal be accepted. All proposals should be submitted online via the PCA/ACA website: http://pcaaca.org More information about the submission process can be found here: https://pcaaca.org/page/submissionguidelines Inquiries about possible papers or proposals for round table sessions or full panels (including those involving the conference theme mentioned above) are also welcomed and encouraged. For themed paper sessions, each presenter must enter her/his own presentation and then contact the area chair to assemble them into a panel. All presenters must be current members of the PCA in order to submit, and must register for the conference in order to present. More detailed information about various conference matters can be found at: https://pcaaca.org/page/2027conf and elsewhere on the PCA website (check the site menus for specific topics). Please feel free to get in touch if you have any questions about topics, process, or the conference in general. Kevin M.
