items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: Framing the Human in the Nineteenth Century 48th Annual Conference Nineteenth-Century Studies Association Philadelphia, PA March 11-13, 2027 Conference website: https://ncsaweb.net/2027-conference-information/ Call for Proposals Submission Deadline: October 31, 2026 Notification of Acceptance: January 2027 Please submit proposals via this Google Form Questions? Email the conference organizers at ncsa2027conference@gmail.com The Nineteenth-Century Studies Association (NCSA) invites proposals for 15-minute papers (300-word proposal) or complete panels of 3-4 papers (600-word proposal) that examine the shifting meanings and status of "the human" in the long nineteenth century-a period shaped by transformative scientific, social, and philosophical developments that continue to inform present-day thought. During this time, evolutionary theory and social Darwinism challenged the boundaries between humans and animals and raised new questions about human difference across race, class, and ethnicity. Theological and philosophical discourses reevaluated humanity's relationship to the divine, while pseudosciences such as phrenology, physiognomy, and anthropometry sought to codify human variation through tools of measurement often aligned with colonial and racial hierarchies. Advances in the natural sciences speculated on human origins and extraterrestrial life, situating "the human" within a larger cosmic framework. Industrialization redefined labor and bodily limits, generating anxieties about overpopulation, and paradoxically, race suicide and population extinction. Amid these pressures, labor and voting rights movements gained momentum, as marginalized groups fought for full inclusion. We welcome proposals from a variety of disciplines that engage with these and other transformations that redefined what it meant to be human-and to belong to humanity-across the long nineteenth century. Topics may include, but are not limited to: The influence of evolutionary theory on concepts of the human and the human/animal divide, including artistic and literary responses Scientific efforts to define human origins and difference through anthropology, racial theory, and other emerging disciplines Population anxieties related to degeneration, overpopulation, and demographic change Emancipated and enslaved bodies The effects of industrialization and technological advancement on understandings of the human body, labor, and automation The rise of the human sciences-psychology, physiology, and medicine-and new approaches to the mind and self Migration and the movement of people, and their impact on ideas of race, nation, and identity Secularization and shifting relationships between the human and the divine Changing human relationships to the environment and the nonhuman world Human rights, labor, and suffrage movements and the redefinition of personhood Transformations in education and access to knowledge The role of cultural institutions (museums, libraries, exhibitions) in shaping public and humanist discourse

items.fullDescription: THE RISE OF ASIA 100 YEARS AFTER LAI: Is the Imperialism Dying and a New World Order Emerging? INTERNATIONAL AND INTERDISCIPLINARY CONFERENCE Paris, February 17, 2027 Le Havre, February 18-19, 2027 https://bandungspirit.org/ CALL FOR ABSTRACTS AND FOR PARTICIPATION The conference is open to individual and group paper presentations. Those willing to present their papers are invited to submit their abstracts until July 31, 2026 (for a possible publication in an edited volume to be launched during the conference) or October 31, 2026 (for a paper presentation in the conference). The notification of selected abstracts for publication or for presentation will be communicated to their authors progressively according to their availability. The earlier the abstracts are submitted, the sooner the authors will get notified. A certain number of selected abstracts may be published as an edited volume to be launched during the conference. The terms of reference is available at https://bandungspirit.org/IMG/pdf/the_rise_of_asia-2027-cfa-a-with-cover.pdf Abstracts of 200-300 words are to be submitted online at https://forms.gle/2F3dS1QrDNQTugUs8 OFFLINE AND ONLINE PARTICIPATION The conference will be organised offline (physically) with possible online (virtual) participation following the circumstances. The programme will be based on offline (physical) participants on Paris time zone. INTRODUCTION LAI (League against Imperialism and for National Independence) was not a conference, but an international organisation active from 1927 to 1937 bringing together communists, socialists, nationalists, trade unionists, and pacifists in order to coordinate their myriad 'assaults against empire'. Founded with the support of the Communist International, the LAI at its peak had a membership of several hundred people, from every inhabited continent, among them prominent interwar activists and future heads of state. The organization aspired both to become an international movement and to coordinate specific instances of mass struggle. It was inaugurated by the "First Congress against Colonial Oppression and Imperialism" in Palais d'Egmont Brussels on February 10-14,1927. Its initiator, Willi Münzenberg, a German communist and the chair of the Workers International Relief, invited many personalities from European and American Left and anti-colonial nationalists from the colonised world. The Brussels Congress was attended by 174 people representing 134 organizations from 34 countries. The list of attendees and organizations identifies delegates from the following places: the United States, Mexico, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Peru, Venezuela, 'Central America', Colombia, China, India, the 'Dutch East Indies' [Indonesia], Korea, 'Indo-China (Annam)', Persia, the Philippines, South Africa, 'West Africa' [Sierra Leone], 'North Africa' [Lamine Senghor, from Senegal, representing the Comité de Défense de la Race Nègre], Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Germany, England, France, Holland, Czechoslovakia, Austria, Italy, Syria, and Palestine. Among those present in Brussels were emissaries of the Chinese Kuomintang party in Europe, Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress, accompanied by Virendranath Chattopadhyaya, Josiah Tshangana Gumede of the African National Congress (ANC) of South Africa, Messali Hadj of the Algerian Étoile Nord-Africaine, and Mohammad Hatta of the Perhimpoenan Indonesia. Moreover, many activists from the European and American Left were present, such as Fenner Brockway, Arthur MacManus, Edo Fimmen, Reginald Bridgeman, and Gabrielle Duchêne, as well as intellectuals such as Henri Barbusse, Romain Rolland, and Albert Einstein. Today, 100 years after LAI, the recent wars in Ukraine and in West Asia (Iran, Israel, Arab countries, USA) raise questions: is the imperialism dying and a new world order emerging? Why? In what way? And what new world order is emerging? Those fundamental questions may be broken down into more specific questions, such as: • Brussels 1927, Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961, Havana 1966, what ruptures and what continuities? • In what ways colonialism, neo-colonialism and imperialism continue to take place? • What impacts of foreign military bases on socio-cultural, economic, environmental and political life of the hosting countries? • What role NAM, BRICS, SCO and other Non-Western institutions play in the changing world order? • Are Marxism, Leninism, Maoism, Nasserism, Sukarnoism still relevant today? • Is socialism still promising to replace capitalism? • What role played by social movements and other non-state actors movements in the fight for human emancipation? • Is the present UN still relevant to the global challenges today? What is necessary? UN reform or UN replacement by a new structure? It is to discuss those such questions that the 11th edition of the Rise of Asia Conference Series is organised. It encourages the participation of scholars from a wide range of scientific disciplines (area studies, cultural studies, ecology, economics, geography, built environment, architecture, urban studies, history, humanities, languages, management, political and social sciences, international relations…) and practitioners from diverse professional fields (business, civil society, education, enterprise, government, management, parliament, public policy, social and solidarity movements…) as well as artists and writers, based in diverse geographical areas (Africa, North, Central and South America, Australia, Asia, the Caribbean, Europe, Oceania, Pacific…). (Darwis Khudori, Conference Initiator and Convenor)

items.fullDescription: Travelling Cultural Heritage Circulation and Digital Afterlives Call for Papers Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference 4th edition Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, Romania December 10-11, 2026 Lucian Blaga University of Sibiu, as part of the FORTHEM Alliance, invites scholars, researchers, and practitioners to submit proposals for the 4th edition of the Cultural Heritage Lab International Conference, dedicated to exploring cultural heritage as a dynamic process of circulation across cultural, geographical, institutional, and historical boundaries. The 2026 edition focuses on Travelling Cultural Heritage (TCH): an approach that understands heritage not as a fixed repository, but as a process through which cultural forms, practices, ideas, and meanings move, encounter different contexts, and are transformed along the way. Drawing on Edward Said's concept of "travelling theory", Mieke Bal's "travelling concepts", and scholarship on cultural circulation, TCH shifts attention from mobile objects to the processes through which heritage is transmitted, adapted, appropriated, reinterpreted, and re-signified. Heritage travels through migration, exchange, conquest, education, trade, tourism, collecting, translation, transmedial transfer, and institutional networks. Migrants adapt cultural practices acquired abroad to their home contexts; travelling elites import fashions, recipes, and other cultural products; artistic styles acquire regional forms as they circulate; and networks of institutions, scholars, dealers, and historical circumstances determine how artefacts enter major collections. Such movements involve adaptation and transformation, but also appropriation, exclusion, and unequal centre-periphery relations. Circulation may allow heritage to acquire new meanings, but it may also entail loss. The large-scale purchase, digitisation, and destruction of books for AI training suggests a future in which physical heritage disappears while its digital avatars survive-an extreme form of travel across media and material states, combining virtual preservation with material destruction. More optimistically, AI, data science, interoperable infrastructures, and spatial visualisation can trace cultural circulation, compare contexts, and recover seemingly lost artefacts, including previously unreadable ancient manuscripts. We welcome contributions that engage with Travelling Cultural Heritage from disciplinary and interdisciplinary perspectives, including cultural and heritage studies, anthropology, archaeology, sociology, history, linguistics and literary studies, political science, art history, architecture, digital humanities, economics, media studies, religious studies, drama, film, the performing arts, museum studies, memory studies, and food studies . Contributors are invited to submit abstracts on, but not limited to, the following themes: Travelling Cultural Heritage: theories, concepts, and methodologies; Cultural circulation, transmission, adaptation, and re-signification; Heritage: migration, displacement, and diaspora; Museums, collections, objects, routes, networks, intermediaries, and infrastructures of cultural circulation; The movement of architectural forms, artistic practices, rituals, and cultural traditions; Colonial, postcolonial, and decolonial circulations of cultural heritage; Digital heritage, digital infrastructures, AI, platforms and computational approaches to cultural circulation; Heritage in translation: what changes when cultural forms travel between languages and the production of new heritage meanings Local content, foreign forms: adaptation and naturalisation across literatures; World Cultural Heritage: comparative approaches to heritage beyond national frameworks; Archaeological evidence for mobility, exchange, and cultural contacts; Memory and heritage: overlappings and differences; Case studies of cultural forms, practices, objects, ideas, or meanings that have travelled across contexts. Submission Guidelines Please submit an abstract of 250-300 words , along with a short biographical note ( max. 100 words ), to Ovio Olaru ( ovio.olaru@ulbsibiu.ro ) and Daniela Stanciu-P?sc?ri?a ( daniela.stanciu@ulbsibiu.ro ) by November 1, 2026. The organisers' decision regarding submissions will be communicated by November 15. For effectiveness, please include " Cultural Heritage Lab conference submission " in the subject line of your email. The conference will be held in English, German, and French, and will take place exclusively on-site. We look forward to your contributions! Kind regards, The organisers

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: [Children's and Young Adult Literature] at CEA 2027 Apr. 1-3, 2027 | St. Louis, Missouri The Westin St. Louis Hotel https://cea-web.org/the-conference-hotel The College English Association, a gathering of scholar-teachers in English studies, welcomes proposals for presentations on Children's and Young Adult Literature for our 57th annual conference. Submit your proposal at www.cea-web.org Scholars and teachers of children's and YA lit intimately know the transformative power the right story at the right time can have on an elementary, middle, or high school student. We do not need reminding of how words, and how they are communicated, to young learners have the ability to grow cognitive processes and lead to future generations of lovers of the written word and future torchbearers of the significance of those words coming from the minds of human beings. Coalescing around the conference theme, we consider how the influence of diverse sculpted stories opens the door to deeper discernment across the curriculum. Conference Theme: Gateways For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Tracing its history back to French explorers in the second half of the 18th century, the great city of St. Louis began as a fur trading post named after King Louis IX of France and was established on the ancestral lands of the Osage Nation, Missouria, and Illini Confederacy. Becoming part of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the city famously came to be known as the "Gateway to the West," serving as a launching point for generations of explorers and settlers expanding the frontier. Yet, we must remember that the city also serves as a gateway to its past as part of indigenous lands transformed through its colonial history into a major river port and trading center that fostered migration both outwards and inwards for centuries. Today, St. Louis invites us to reflect on the continued significance of gateways in our 21st-century lives. GENERAL CALL FOR PAPERS GATEWAYS: For its 2027 annual conference, the College English Association (CEA) invites proposals for papers and panels that explore the theme of "Gateways" and their significance in literature, criticism, and pedagogy. Potential areas of interest: How do gateways expand literary and cultural spaces but also, as access points, mark out boundaries and limits? Do gateways invite gatekeepers to enable and limit access? Is it possible to imagine gateways without gatekeepers? How can we imagine literary and cultural gateways to foster inter-cultural, cross-cultural, and trans-cultural interactions? How do we envision pedagogical approaches to create gateways for our students to new literary vistas, critical thought, and professional opportunities? How can gateways in both their physical and symbolic significances (like the city of St. Louis and the Gateway Arch) connect the territorial to the cultural, imaginative, and spiritual in literary-critical studies? In what ways can we re-imagine our scholarly and pedagogical work to open up interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary gateways? For CEA 2027, we are especially interested topics related to GATEWAYS in texts, disciplines, people, cultural studies, media, and pedagogy. Consider such topics as the implications of political gateways across time and place, cultural gateways of identity, gateways in the media (including social media) and how they impact society, pedagogical gateways of teaching philosophy and their implementation, or personal gateways through autobiography and memoir. GENERAL TOPICS: The CEA Conference encompasses a wide range of areas, including literary studies, creative writing, rhetoric and composition, technical communication, linguistics, and film. We further encourage proposals in areas about our wider role as academics, including student/instructor accountability and assessment, student advising, academic leadership in departments and programs, and the place of the English department in the university. NEW FOR 2027: UNDERGRADUATE ROUNDTABLES CEA invites undergraduates to enjoy the conference experience by sharing their work in flash-essay roundtable sessions. A flash essay is a highly condensed, high-impact presentation (typically 300-1000 words, or 2-5 minutes) that delivers core research findings, a specific argument, or a compelling narrative. During roundtable sessions, the speakers and audience engage in discussion with each other in more of an open conversation than in traditional panels. Learn more about roundtables here: https://cea-web.org/about-roundtables. For additional information or discussion about this topic and its panels, please contact Peter Elliott at pselliott@anderson.edu.

items.fullDescription: WANT TO EDIT AN ISSUE OF A JOURNAL? • The Journal of Undergraduate Research in the Humanities (JURH) is looking for guest editors for our Summer 2027 issue. WHAT IS JURH? • JURH is an annual journal that provides a national forum to showcase the best in undergraduate Humanities research. Click here to learn more about JURH. • JURH is governed by a board of nationally recognized scholars and overseen by Dr. Lara Karpenko, Professor of English, and Director of the Center for the Humanities at Carroll University and Dr. Lauri Dietz, Executive Director, Center for Faculty Development, Loyola University, Chicago. • In even years (2024, 2026, etc.), JURH is run by an editorial team of undergraduates. In odd years, the journal hosts a themed special issue from a guest editor or editorial team. WHO CAN APPLY AND WHAT IS EXPECTED? • Guest Editors can be graduate students, staff, or faculty from any 2- or 4-year institution in the United States or around the world. • Note that we will also consider undergraduate editors as long as they have a committed faculty or staff member to support them through the process. Faculty or staff member should be named on the application. • In addition to single-editor proposals, we are also happy to consider editorial teams of 2 to 4. • Editors are expected to write the CFP, advertise the CFP (with support from the JURH board), accept and decline submissions, work with authors to get the essays submission-ready, write the issue introduction, copyedit all material, and format the issue according to JURH specifications. • The complete issue will be due to JURH by July 1, 2027. • Issues should be themed and feature undergraduate work. Occasionally, however, the themed issue can feature work from other writing populations. See, for instance, our themed second issue which features the work of high school researchers and that also includes a round table discussion between high school educators. HOW TO APPLY? • All prospective editors should send proposals in an email attachment to Dr. Lara Karpenko at lkarpenk@carrollu.edu by November 1, 2026. Proposals should explain: -The proposed theme and why it's relevant to JURH -Who the intended writers are -If any authors are already lined up -Where the editors intend to circulate the CFP -A proposed timeline for completion of work • Prospective editors should also send brief bios and/or CVs that explain any experience in editing or project management. (Note that experience isn't required.) Please submit one bio or CV for each editor. For more info, go to https://jurh.net/call-for-editors/

items.fullDescription: Confound the Time welcomes papers that investigate the ways in which texts, objects, and images from the medieval and early modern periods re-envision and reconstruct the past or imagine and anticipate the future. We also welcome papers that explore the ways in which medieval and early modern artifacts, history, and culture are reimagined and reconstructed in later periods. As part of our commitment to accessibility, Confound the Time will be entirely virtual and have no registration fee. Graduate students and early career scholars are especially encouraged to submit. Topics for individual papers may include: Medieval and early modern reception of classical mythology/culture Early modern reception of medieval literature/culture The Pre-Raphaelites and other neo-medievalist movements Contemporary video games, graphic novels, television shows, and/or films with medieval or early modern settings, characters, and cultures Dungeons and Dragons and/or other role-playing or tabletop games Manuscript Studies/Book History Time/The Times Gender and Sexuality Nationalism and Race Papers that address these subjects are encouraged, but any paper that centers on medieval or early modern studies will be considered. Please fill out this form to the best of your ability in order to submit: https://forms.gle/B8YhxejNzQHGsfcV8 The deadline for all abstract submissions is November 7th, 2026. The virtual conference will be held from February 6th-February 7th 2027. Questions can be directed to Drs. This international academic event seeks to bring together researchers, academics, artists, educators, and professionals from different disciplines to explore the historical, cultural, social, artistic, scientific, and technological dimensions of healing and well-being. The Congress proposes a dialogue between nineteenth-century traditions and contemporary approaches to health and healing, examining continuities, transformations, exchanges, and tensions across the Hispanic world, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which literature, art, spirituality, traditional medicine, bodily practices, digital technologies, and community experiences have shaped understandings and practices of healing. Suggested themes include: Genealogies of Healing in Nineteenth-Century Hispanic Culture Representations of Illness in Nineteenth-Century Literature and the Press Art and Healing: Music, Dance, Painting, and Theatre as Therapeutic Practices Dialogues between Allopathic Medicine and Traditional Healing Systems Spirituality, Religion, and Healing Practices Healing through Words: Narratives, Discourse, and Therapeutic Processes Convergences between Bodily Practices (Yoga, Pranayama, Sports) and Holistic Health Healing Traditions in Asia and the Caribbean: Exchanges with the Hispanic World Digital Health, Applications, Platforms, and Well-Being Monitoring Ethical and Clinical Risks of Chatbots and Mental Health Technologies Social Media, Virality, and Their Impact on Emotional Health Attention, Cognition, and Technology Digital Churches, the Spiritual Economy, and New Forms of Religiosity Education and Well-Being Public Health Policies in Digital and Multicultural Environments Interdisciplinarity in Health: Intersections between Art, Science, and Technology Imaginaries of Good and Evil in Processes of Illness and Healing Community Well-Being and Territorial Experiences Researchers interested in participating are invited to submit proposals in accordance with the Congress guidelines. items.fullDescription: CFP: 28th Southeast Conference for Languages, Literatures, and Film (Feb 27-28, 2027) in St. Petersburg, Florida (on the University of South Florida St. Petersburg Campus) Languages and Cultures in a Changing World: Identity, Responsibility, and Justice Abstracts for papers (and panels) are now being considered. Deadline for abstracts: Nov. 16, 2026 Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. To view prior publication, visit the conference website. The SCFLLF welcomes papers on all aspects of literature, theoretical and applied linguistics, culture, philosophy, cultural history, film, other popular media, second language acquisition, and language pedagogy pertaining to non-English languages (ancient and modern). We would like to encourage (but not limit) submissions addressing our conference theme: Identity, Responsibility and Justice, in its broadest understanding. Selected papers will be published in a post-conference anthology. The humanities and the study of languages are facing changing institutional and social expectations. These changes encourage us to reconsider what work we do and the people and communities our work serves. To whom and to what, are artists, scholars and teachers accountable? How do languages, literatures, films, and other forms of cultural expression preserve or challenge established narratives and structures? How do they engage with different identities? How can they help us understand the present and/or imagine different futures? What responsibilities come with teaching and learning languages as well as with studying, interpreting, and representing other cultures? This conference invites scholars working in non-English languages, literatures, film and media, cultural studies, applied and theoretical linguistics, second-language acquisition, and language pedagogy to explore these and related questions from a wide range of disciplinary, theoretical, historical, and methodological perspectives. The conference theme, Identity, Responsibility, and Justice, is deliberately broad. Responsibility may involve our relationships with students and communities, with texts and their histories, with linguistic and cultural traditions, or with the institutions in which we teach and conduct research. Or responsibility can be interrogated with regard to artists and art, in a broad sense. Justice can also be approached in diverse ways. It may involve social justice, questions of representation and recognition, historical memory, inclusion and exclusion, or access and lack thereof to language learning. Justice may also concern translation and cultural mediation or the ways in which literature, film, language, and other cultural practices engage with conflict, inequality, trauma, discrimination, displacement, and/or social change. The SCFLLF keynote speaker is Adam Schwartz (Associate Professor of Language, Culture & Society, Oregon State University). Dr. Schwartz's research addresses Spanish language education and Spanish-English multilingualisms in the U.S. He takes particular interest in intersections of language, race and racism, wherein questions of identity, responsibility and justice persist. In addition to various articles and chapters, he has authored three books. These include Spanish So White: Conversations on the Inconvenient Racism of a 'Foreign' Language Education (2023). He is also the co-author of Aquí se habla: Centering the Local and Personal in Spanish Language Education (2025) as well as Language, Identity and Justice: The Anthropolitical Worlds of Ana Celia Zentella (2026). Some suggestions of topics and their artistic representations include: identity, responsibility, and justice represented in literature, art, film, and other forms of popular media, including social media influence of film and literature on the public and private sphere reassessing the purpose and value of language teaching expressions and perceptions of trauma in response to injustice justice in utopian fictional worlds addressing and expressing identity in the language classroom questions of identity in literature, film, the arts, and other popular media responsibility issues in production and reception of artistic expressions responsibilities associated with researching and representing cultures apart or in comparison to our own the broader influence of imaginary worlds created in film, literature, the visual arts, and other forms of media on real political and personal justice language and linguistic-related topics concerning identity, responsibility, and justice other topics Please submit a proposal (of no more than 250 words) for a single paper or a full panel (max. of 3 presentations) on the conference webpage. We can only accept online submissions. Please contact Margit Grieb (grieber@usf.edu) if you have any questions.

items.fullDescription: Overview | South Mediterranean University, Tunisia Hybrid Format: In-person and Online Participation The SMU Conference on AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms will take place at South Mediterranean University, Tunisia. This research oriented event brings together scholars, educators, instructional designers, and researchers to explore evidence-based pedagogical innovation in technology-mediated and AI-enhanced learning environments. This conference provides an international platform to present academic research, foster interdisciplinary dialogue, and advance collaboration on the future of teaching and learning in the AI era. The 2027 SMU Conference, themed "AI-Era Teaching: Innovative Pedagogy and Reimagined Classrooms," examines how AI and emerging educational technologies reshape instructional design, classroom engagement, assessment, and learning ecosystems. Key focus areas include measurable learning outcomes, ethical and inclusive AI integration, pedagogical quality assurance, and student competency development in hybrid and digital environments. We invite researchers, practitioners, instructional designers, and graduate students worldwide to submit original research, empirical studies, and case studies on innovative pedagogy, AI-enhanced instruction, learning analytics, engagement strategies, and inclusive practices.

items.fullDescription: Call for Essays, September 2026 Entanglements: Regimes of Extraction and The Literary Imagination of Place Co-editors: Dr. Gayathri Goel and Dr. Jennifer Horwitz The constellation of essays in this collection will focus on place-based literary works and address issues around resource extraction and ecological devastation. As the foremost cause of underdevelopment and ecological destruction in the Global South and many parts of North America, resource extraction, its resulting land loss and labor exploitation, is the occasion for this project. One of the aims of this collection is to expand "resource extraction" beyond the primary focus on extraction of fossil fuels, natural gas, and minerals and includes the commodification of any part of nature that results in impoverishment and harm without any consideration for sustainability, renewability, and justice for humans and nonhumans. The utilization and/or extraction of resources is a regular aspect of human activity for the purposes of subsistence to ensure the continued progression of human society. However, the essays in this collection will treat resource extraction as a reference to imperialist "extractivism" that depletes resources for profit, steadily impoverishing entire communities, accelerating environmental devastation, and deepening local conflicts. Central to this project is also "place" and a deep engagement with literatures that are situated in specific places around the world. As environmental issues are rooted in specific ecological practices, politics, cultures, and history, and also vary widely in nature and severity, an attention to place, then, serves as an anchor and a critical framework for complex analysis. We invite papers that can contribute to this divergent field of "place studies" by centering marginalized voices from across the globe. The accepted papers will address place-based extractivism and/or resistance to issues of exploitation of any part of an environmental community, land and habitat loss, resource scarcity, displacement/migration, collapsing interdependencies from various parts of the world, from the Pacific Islands, Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, to the Americas. The essays will use any combination of critical lenses/perspectives including, Black, Indigenous, feminist, anti-racist, anti-capitalist, decolonization thought to envision lively and liberated places for life forms beyond human and plant, animal, and avian inhabitants. Note: At this point, we are accepting essays only on African, Latin American, Pacific Ocean literatures for the collection. Please submit a 9000-word draft (including notes and citations), along with a 300-word abstract, by December 1st, 2026 to placebasedliteratures@gmail.com. Please feel free to reach out to the editors at the same email for your queries about the timeline or for any other clarifications regarding this project.

items.fullDescription: Social Inclusion, peer-reviewed journal indexed in the Social Sciences Citation Index and Scopus, welcomes new and exciting research papers for its upcoming issue "Inclusive Diversity in European Education: From Policy Frameworks to Classroom Practices," edited by Roberto Baelo Álvarez, Alessandro Bergamaschi, and Anna Elia. Submission of Abstracts: 1-15 December 2026 Submission of Full Papers: 15-30 April 2027 Publication of the Issue: June/December 2027 About the issue: Contemporary European societies are characterised by an unprecedented degree of diversity (linguistic, cultural, ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic), challenging the foundations of traditional educational systems. The concept of superdiversity, which moves beyond binary majority-minority frameworks to account for the complex intersectionality of identities and trajectories, reflects the lived reality of classrooms, schools, and universities across the continent. However, educational policies and pedagogical practices have often lagged behind this transformation, generating tensions between normative aspirations for inclusion and the structural conditions shaping everyday educational contexts. This thematic issue brings together interdisciplinary scholarship examining how educational systems across Europe and beyond are responding, or failing to respond, to the challenges and opportunities posed by diversity. Drawing on sociology, educational science, political science, and intercultural studies, the issue addresses four interconnected dimensions: the normative and policy frameworks governing diversity in education; the social implications of superdiversity for educational communities, particularly the tension between demands for equality and differentiation in everyday school situations; the pedagogical approaches, teacher education strategies, and curricular innovations aimed at fostering inclusive learning environments; and the perspectives of key actors, including students, educators, institutions, and civil society. Finally, the issue aims to critically examine whether inclusion can be considered a new paradigm for understanding social cohesion, alongside established models such as multiculturalism and assimilationism, and their respective contributions to the educational field. The issue welcomes original research, systematic reviews, and theoretically grounded contributions that engage with multiculturalism, intercultural education, diversity management, social cohesion, and inclusive educational practice in formal and non-formal settings across all educational levels. Comparative, cross-national, and transdisciplinary perspectives are particularly encouraged, as are contributions documenting good practices and innovative approaches. By bringing these conversations into dialogue, this issue advances scholarly understanding and evidence-based policy reflection on one of the most pressing challenges facing European and global educational systems today. Instructions for authors: Authors interested in submitting a paper for this issue are asked to consult the journal's instructions for authors and submit their abstracts (maximum of 250 words, with a tentative title) through the abstracts system: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/app/socialinclusion/abstracts When submitting their abstracts, authors are also asked to confirm that they are aware that Social Inclusion is an open access journal with a publishing fee if the article is accepted for publication after peer-review (corresponding authors affiliated with our institutional members do not incur this fee). Open access: Readers across the globe will be able to access, share, and download this issue entirely for free. Corresponding authors affiliated with any of our institutional members (over 100 institutions worldwide) publish free of charge. Otherwise, an article processing fee will be charged to the authors to cover editorial costs. We defend that authors should not have to personally pay this fee and encourage them to check with their institutions if funds are available to cover open access publication costs. Further information about the journal's open access charges can be found here: https://www.cogitatiopress.com/socialinclusion/about/editorialPolicies#publicationFees Abstracts welcome until 15 December 2026.

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers Yearbook KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE VOL. 32 (2027) (Göttingen: V&R unipress/Universitätsverlag Osnabrückpublished since 1989 and as a yearbook since 2000; distributed to subscribers worldwide) Invisible Fronts - Representations of War between AI, Disinformation, and Hybrid Warfare Wars have never been fought solely on military battlefields. Cyber operations, social media, automated weapons systems, algorithmic decision-making processes, and generative artificial intelligence have transformed warfare in recent decades-as well as its media representation and public perception. Disinformation, surveillance, and the deliberate manipulation of public perception are increasingly blurring the lines between war and peace, reality and simulation, and documentation and staging. The 2027 issue of KRIEG UND LITERATUR/WAR AND LITERATURE explores cultural representations of these developments. The focus is on how 20th- and 21st-century media depict, reflect on, critique, or anticipate technological and hybrid forms of warfare, and how new technologies are changing the conditions under which wars are narrated, documented, remembered, and perceived as real. Possible topics include: • AI, autonomous weapons systems, drones, and algorithmic targeting; • cyberwarfare, hybrid warfare, and digital infrastructures; • propaganda, disinformation, and deepfakes; • generative AI and synthetic images of war; • manipulation of perception, memory, and enemy stereotypes; • responsibility and agency in the relationship between humans and machines; • historical imaginaries of automated and hybrid warfare. Across all genres and formats, contributions may examine works and materials from literature, film and television, comics and graphic novels, visual and digital art, photography, social media, and video games. Interdisciplinary, comparative, and transnational approaches are also welcome. Contributions may be submitted in German or English . The following general formatting guidelines should be observed: • Submit as a WORD or RTF document; language: German or English; a maximum of 25 A4 pages (excluding illustrations); Footnotes rather than endnotes); • Figures (printed in black and white) must be submitted separately as offset film, a reproducible original, or in digital format (*.tif, *.jpg with at least 300 dpi in CMYK mode). Please mark the location in the text where each figure is to appear. Do not embed the figures in the document; • Include correct and complete figure captions in the text or in a separate file; • Authors are responsible for obtaining all necessary reproduction permissions. Detailed "Guidelines for Authors" will be sent separately. Abstracts : 1,500-2,000 characters (including spaces) Deadline for abstract submissions : December 31, 2026 Notification of acceptance : January 31, 2027 Deadline for full paper submission : June 30, 2027 Paper length : 15-25 pages Contact and Submission : Claudia Junk, M.A. and Alice Cadeddu, M.A. (Editors) Email: junk@osnabrueck.de; cadeddu@osnabrueck.de Erich Maria Remarque Peace Center; www.remarque.de

items.fullDescription: Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium April 7th-April 9th 2027 Arizona State University Many scholars argue that we are now living in a new geological epoch-the Anthropocene-a name chosen to encapsulate an irreversibly transformed planet due to the rapid expansion of human populations, increasing exploitation of animals and natural resources, and pervasive pollution. The effects of the Anthropocene have been caused by only a small percentage of the world's population, yet those living in the Global South disproportionately suffer the consequences. The Anthropocene, then, is just as much a social problem as it is an environmental issue. Despite the centrality of animals to planetary health, however, nonhuman life often remains peripheral to discussions of climate and environmental sustainability, even as industrial agriculture drives deforestation and carbon emissions, species extinction destabilizes ecosystems, and the increasing emergence of zoonotic diseases-Covid-19 and Hantavirus among them-reveals the profound interdependence of human, animal, and environmental health. At the same time, dominant responses to environmental crises, which made possible the conditions of crisis in the first place, tend to privilege scientific discovery and technological innovation while neglecting the cultural narratives, entrenched biases, and networks of power that shape human-animal relationships.. To that end, imagining more just and hospitable futures requires new interdisciplinary approaches that recognize animals and interspecies relations as critical to collective flourishing and environmental sustainability. The Animal Studies Across Disciplines Symposium will bring together scholars, artists, students, animal professionals, and community members across the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences to discuss animals and multispecies futures. The symposium is designed not only as a scholarly gathering, but as the start of a long-term collaborative network capable of shaping future research, public humanities work, community partnerships, and environmental dialogue. The inaugural Spring 2027 Symposium will center on the keyword "care," inviting participants to analyze how different disciplines, professions, and communities define and mobilize care in relation to animals, multispecies justice, and environmental stewardship. In doing so, the Symposium will evaluate practices of protection and responsibility alongside the violences and inequalities that shape life across species. For example, how might a humanities scholar, veterinarian, ecologist, or activist understand and practice care differently, and what might each learn from the knowledge, methods, and questions of the others? How might regional, place-based, and communal forms of knowledge offer different ways of understanding our relationships and responsibilities to animals? How is care negotiated when the welfare of an individual animal comes into conflict with the preservation of a population, species, or ecosystem? What might care mean for animals such as insects, whose small size, vast numbers, and frequent classification as pests or disease vectors complicate familiar practices of care? How do animals care for themselves, one another, and members of other species, and what might these practices teach us about caring for each other and the more-than-human world? The Symposium invites participants to consider what becomes possible when different ways of knowing and relating to animals are brought into conversation, and how such exchanges might expand our understanding and practice of care across species. items.fullDescription: The Journal for the New Narratives in the History of Philosophy (JNNHP) invites submissions for its special on Derrick Bell and the History of Africana Philosophy, to be published in Fall 2027. Derrick Bell, the founder of Critical Race Theory, produced one of the most innovative, insightful, and transformative ideas in the 20th century. His philosophical insights continue to challenge how western liberal nations contend with questions of civil rights, human rights, immigration, policing, and education. Recent conservative attacks focused on Critical Race Theory (CRT) in the U.S, Canada, and England assert, albeit erroneously, that CRT is a Marxist and communist ideology that seeks to supplant western values and the ethos of liberal democracy. Contrary to these fallacious attacks, Bell's textbook Race, Racism, and American Law is amongst the first law textbooks to give a comprehensive view of how racism shaped the development of American law and race relations. In this regard, CRT draws heavily on a tradition of Africana philosophy from slavery through the 20th century. It challenges, not only the supposed neutrality of U.S. law, but also the universality of western political ideals, and U.S. law as egalitarian. For example, Bell engaged Frederick Douglass's critiques of natural law theorists and abolitionists who read the American Constitution as a slave document. For Douglass, the Constitution is an economic contract that robs slaves of their labour and property rights. Drawing on Douglass' critique, Bell interrogated how economic interests have structured American law as an instrument for white class interests over Black claims for justice from slavery through the 20th century. Similarly, Bell engaged W.E.B DuBois's reading of American democracy that underscored how U.S. law in the 13 colonies suppressed African revolts while upholding slavery. Such legal resistance to African acts of liberation, Dubois argued, created paradoxes for American democracy and shaped how the legal system understood the Black freedom struggle. Following Dubois' analysis, Bell explored how the law is an ineffective tool for racial remediation when it comes to addressing social injustices that confront Black life. Bell also engaged Malcolm X's critiques of the Reconstruction era civil rights and 1960 civil rights amendments as pyrrhic victories. This inspired Bell to think about how civil rights function as symbolic victories while ensuring racism is a permanent fixture of American democracy. Given Bell's extensive engagement with 18th-20th century Africana philosophy, this special seeks to consider Bell's work within Africana philosophy. As such, the special welcomes essays that focus on Bell's work as philosophical historiography and inquiry into Black life and its relation to democracy as part of the long tradition of Africana philosophy. The special seeks contributions that address the following themes: Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black history. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black legal theory. Derrick Bell and the Black Nationalist and the Black Radical Tradition. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of Black Education. Derrick Bell as a philosopher of contemporary society and issue of civil rights. Essays must be submitted to https://journal.lib.uoguelph.ca/index.php/nnhp/about/submissions Deadline for Essay Submission: January 7th, 2027. Papers will be considered after January 7th, 2027. The Co-lead Guest Editors for this Special are Drs. Dalitso Ruwe (Queens University), Adebayo Oluwayomi (West Chester University), Andrew Soto (Hartnell College). For questions about the Special, please contact: derrickbellspecial@gmail.com JNNHP is an open-access online journal committed to publishing papers on underrepresented figures or themes in the history of philosophy, both Western and non-Western traditions, from the ancient period to the mid-20th century. items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals The editorial and scientific board of the journal Co-herencia invites researchers, professors, and scholars affiliated with national or international institutions to submit proposals for thematic issues/dossiers, and to apply to serve as Guest Scientific Editors for Volume 25, Issue 48 (covering the period January-June 2028). Presentation and Scientific Scope of the Journal Co-herencia Co-herencia is an indexed scientific journal, published biannually, under Diamond Open Access with a CC BY 4.0 license, and edited by the School of Arts and Humanities at EAFIT University. Indexed in major international databases such as Scopus (Arts & Humanities, Q2 SJR), Co-herencia ensures methodological rigor, double-blind peer review, and high ethical publishing standards. The journal is published in Spanish, English, and Portuguese. Published without interruption since 2004, the journal aims to serve as a forum for interdisciplinary discussion on the contributions of the humanities and the arts to the shaping of a thoughtful, critical, and deliberative community. Its scope and thematic axes are concentrated mainly on: Literary Studies: Literary theory; Literary genres; Classical tradition; Hermeneutics; Canon, criticism, and history of literature in the Americas; Writing and orality; Translation; Reception; Literary creation; Semiotics; Editing studies; Journalism and literature; Applied literature. Arts: Mediality, transmediality, and intermediality; Creative industries; Musicology; History of music; Material and visual culture; Curatorship and museography; Sociology of the arts; Interartistic relations; Avant-gardes and artistic movements; Canon, criticism, and history of the arts in the Americas. Requirements for Submitting Proposals In keeping with international editorial best practices in the field of Arts and Humanities (diverse impact, editorial exogamy, international outreach, and analytical rigor), proposals submitted by candidates for guest editors must be presented in a single document (PDF or Word), written in Spanish, English, or Portuguese, and must include, in detail, the following five sections: Title of the thematic issue: it should be concise, clear, conceptually strong, and reflect the central problem to be addressed. Thematic presentation and theoretical grounding (500 to 1,000 words): propose a conceptual delimitation and a definition of the object of study, the core question, or the problematizing axis of the dossier. The proposal should also detail the disciplinary or interdisciplinary frameworks, indicating how the theme and approach engage with the journal's scientific scope. Justification and academic relevance (500 to 1,000 words): include a synthesis of the state of the art and a clear account of the novelty and relevance of the proposal within the contemporary debate in the arts and humanities. This section should ideally state the potential impact and interest the issue will generate within the international research community. Scientific biography of the prospective guest editors: a team of two to three guest editors with diverse institutional affiliations is recommended. For each team member, please indicate: full name, current institutional affiliation, highest academic degree, ORCID iD, and a summary (max. 300 words) of their research lines, ongoing projects, and recent publications in the thematic area of the proposal. Guest editors commit to actively participating in the preselection of manuscripts, suggesting qualified reviewers, and drafting a presentation/introduction for the dossier. items.fullDescription: In his seminal and final film Black Is…Black Ain't , the documentarian Marlon Riggs utilizes a pot of gumbo to articulate his thesis that Blackness necessitates an identity built on multiplicity, complication, and depth (Riggs 1995). Such a vision contests and destabilizes narratives depicted within the film that sought to limit Black identities and identifications, and it cuts against the second half of his title, which suggests Blackness in terms of negation, evasion, and minimization. His articulation becomes not just an evocation of Black identifications but a creation of what a Black identity can be. Riggs continues a conversation with Ralph Ellison, Ama Ata Aidoo, Toni Morrison, Stuart Hall, and centuries of international Black thought. By doubling down on the "is" and considering contradictory, harmonious, and contrapuntal accounts of the many ways Blackness is and can be, the Gregory J. Hampton Graduate English Student Association hopes to join this dialogue with its March 25-26, 2027 conference. We invite papers that contemplate how storytelling produces and shapes Black identities as much as it narrates them, forming, revising, and improvising senses of self and community. This conference also does commemorative work. We are honoring the career of Dr. Jimisha Relerford, a graduate of our program and member of the Howard community who passed recently. Her dissertation broke critical ground in its study of Black women's satire. We thus encourage the submission of papers about Black satire, especially Black women's work in the genre. Writers such as Leone Ross, Danzy Senna, Fran Ross, and Zadie Smith, all of whom were discussed in Dr. Relerford's dissertation, use satire to comment on and transform notions of Blackness. We hope to continue Dr. Relerford's project by reflecting on how storytellers work within this genre to talk about identity. We additionally encourage studies of Afrofuturist and speculative Black texts in reference to our organization's namesake, a pillar in Afrofuturist study. In addition to recognizing the intellectual impacts of Drs. Relerford and Hampton, this conference serves as a milestone, marking the tenth conference our organization has hosted in honor of Black literary study. Given Black academia and HBCUs's influence on identity and storytelling around it, we also welcome papers pondering scholarly impacts on identity as seen in criticism, productions, and protest. We additionally invite papers in the following areas that intersect with identity and identification study in story: African Studies African-American Studies Caribbean Studies Disability Studies Ecocriticism and Ecopoetics Diaspora, Ethnicity, and Migration Studies Food Studies Hip Hop Humor Literary History Protest and Rhetoric Queer Studies Television and Film Theater and Performance To submit a paper or panel to our conference, please email an abstract of 250-300 words to gesasecretary@gmail.com no later than January 15, 2027. In your email include your name, affiliation, contact information, and a brief biographical blurb.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS The Politics of Care in Higher Education: Pedagogies, Communities, and Institutional Tensions Eds. Gretta Sayers, Dominique Hétu, and Mousumi Majumder This edited collection offers a timely contribution to the growing body of scholarship on care in higher education (Child & Marvel, 2023; Johnston, 2024; Evans, 2025; Boden et al., 2026). Moving beyond celebratory narratives that romanticize care, treat it as inherently benevolent, or present it as a natural and uncomplicated good, this volume approaches care as a complex and contested practice shaped by institutional structures, power relations, material conditions, and unequal distributions of labour. It examines how care operates simultaneously as a pedagogical ethic, relational practice, and institutional discourse, while foregrounding the tensions and contradictions that emerge in its enactment in higher education. We seek contributions that examine both the transformative possibilities and the political contradictions of care in academic life, engaging urgent concerns surrounding precarity, burnout, institutional rhetoric, and collective responsibility while offering grounded and theoretically rigorous pathways for reimagining academic communities. Guided by an editorial team working across science, arts, and music, the volume approaches care as a question that exceeds disciplinary boundaries and conventional academic forms. We welcome interdisciplinary contributions exploring pedagogies of care in academia as relational, political, ethical, and institutional practices, and particularly encourage critical perspectives attentive to the tensions between care as transformative praxis and care as institutional discourse. In keeping with this interdisciplinary and expansive orientation, we welcome not only scholarly analysis but also contributions that engage pedagogical and institutional questions through research-creation, creative and arts-based methodologies, embodied and relational inquiry, and other forms of knowledge-making attentive to care, reciprocity, and collective responsibility. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Communities of Practice, Solidarity, and Collective Care Focus on the relationships, networks, and collective structures through which care is enacted, sustained, and negotiated within and beyond academic institutions. Contributions may critically examine communities of practice, mentorship, solidarity, belonging, and collective responses to precarity, exclusion, and institutional change. Communities of practice as spaces of relational learning and mutual support Collective care and solidarity within academic communities Faculty, staff, student, and intergenerational communities of care Mentorship, sponsorship, and peer-support networks Community-based and grassroots care practices Communities of resistance and alternative academic cultures Care infrastructures within and beyond institutions Transnational, intercultural, and multilingual communities of practice Critical and Decolonial Theorizations of Care Feminist, decolonial, anti-racist, Indigenous, disability, queer, and intersectional approaches to care Care as relational, political, ethical, and collective practice Relational accountability, reciprocity, and responsibility Distinctions and tensions between care, compassion, empathy, wellness, and support Decolonizing care and questioning dominant or universalized understandings of care Care, power, and the politics of recognition and belonging Care, Institutions, and Structural Conditions Who is responsible for care? Institutional accountability and the challenges of "walking the talk" The instrumentalization, depoliticization, or weaponization of care "Care-washing," compassionate governance, and institutional contradictions Structural inequities and institutional barriers to caring practices Equity, accessibility, and accountability in institutional approaches to care Care as institutional discourse, managerial language, or policy framework Labour, Power, and Unequal Expectations of Care Gendered, racialized, colonial, and ableist distributions of care labour Emotional, affective, and relational labour in academia Invisible, undervalued, and uncompensated care work Faculty, staff, and student wellbeing beyond individualized frameworks Burnout, exhaustion, and care fatigue Boundaries, refusal, and care without self-erasure Institutional responsibility and the redistribution of care work Care, academic precarity, workload, and cultures of overextension Precarious labour and the politics of academic support Educational Leadership, Governance, and Institutional Contradictions Focus on educational leadership, governance, and institutional decision-making as sites where commitments to care encounter institutional hierarchies, competing responsibilities, material constraints, and unequal relations of power. The tensions between relational leadership and hierarchical authority Who is expected, authorized, or positioned to make decisions about what counts as care and for whom. Institutional commitments to care alongside austerity, restructuring, precarity, workload intensification, and performance management The contradictions of leaders being asked to enact care while administering policies or decisions that may produce harm Care as institutional responsibility versus the individualization or downward delegation of caring labour Governance, consultation, and participation: whose voices are heard, recognized, or excluded in institutional decisions about care Care, accountability, and evaluation: the challenges of recognizing caring practices without rendering care measurable, performative, or managerial Leadership, refusal, and complicity: the limits of care within institutions whose structures may themselves reproduce inequity Research, Knowledge Production, and Ethical Scholarship Focus on care as an epistemological, methodological, and ethical framework for research and knowledge production. Contributions may explore how care shapes scholarly inquiry, research relationships, academic publishing, and the production, circulation, and validation of knowledge. Collaborative, participatory, and community-engaged research methodologies Communities of practice as sites of collective knowledge production Decolonial, Indigenous, and community-accountable research practices Knowledge production, epistemic justice, and the ethics of listening Care as a research methodology and analytical framework The production, negotiation, and contestation of safe spaces in research and educational contexts Slow scholarship and alternative temporalities of knowledge production Critical and Creative Interventions Arts-based and creative approaches to care Case studies of care-based initiatives and institutional tensions Failures, ambivalences, and unintended consequences of care Pedagogies of refusal, repair, and institutional critique Reimagining academic cultures through justice-oriented and decolonial care Futures of care in higher education We particularly welcome contributions that critically and creatively engage the possibilities and limits of care, foreground questions of equity and justice, and explore the conditions under which pedagogies and communities of practice may foster, constrain, or complicate more accountable, inclusive, and transformative academic cultures. Please submit your detailed abstract (max 500 words, in a .docx or PDF file) to carecommunity@brandonu.ca by Jan. 15, 2027 , along with a bio (250 words). Detailed Abstract Requirements Submissions should include a detailed abstract of up to 500 words outlining the proposed contribution. The abstract should present: its central argument, question, or inquiry; its conceptual or theoretical grounding; its methodological and/or creative approach; the texts, creative works, practices, or other materials on which the contribution will draws. Proposals may also take the form of research-creation projects or involve alternative, multimodal, or community-engaged approaches to knowledge production and dissemination. In such cases, the abstract should clearly describe the proposed form and its relevance to the contribution. Contributions should normally range between 4,000 and 8,000 words. Creative and hybrid contributions that take forms for which word count is not the most appropriate measure are invited to discuss format and length with the editors. items.fullDescription: Special Issue Website: https://www.mdpi.com/journal/literature/special_issues/B781Q58SAM Dear Colleagues, This Special Issue of Literature will collect essays addressing the reception, influence, adaptation, or incorporation of literature from the Greco-Roman world into later theatre, film, and television. The Greeks and Romans pioneered a wide range of performed literary styles like tragic and comic drama, or epic and lyric poetry, as well as developing extensive mythic story networks and what we now recognize as formal histories, etc. Some of these works remain among the most influential and beloved writings ever produced by humanity. Because Greco-Roman literature is so culturally powerful and beloved, receptions and uses of it have occurred continually since the Greco-Roman era itself, in myriad different ways. This Issue seeks articles focused on performed receptions, exploring the cultural and artistic politics of how Greco-Roman material is brought to life for viewers, either on stages or screens. The recent controversies about casting and "historical accuracy" with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film remind us of the power and perils of live performance in the evocation of classics, so the articles for this Issue will interrogate the weight of and responses to classics' cultural authority. The Special Issue aims to provide current scholarly arguments about the role and ongoing power of Greek and Roman literature in theatre, film, television, or other performed media, consistent with the broader aims and scope of Literature. Purposefully taking a broad lens, the Issue seeks essays focused across time periods (e.g., medieval to the present), different national or regional performances/arts, and across media in order to bring together the most comprehensive body of essays possible. Potential topics include, but are not limited to: Theatrical or performed adaptation of or allusions to Greek and Roman literature within the Greco-Roman world. Medieval European or Middle Eastern reworkings and influence of Greco-Roman poetry or drama. Renaissance or Enlightenment re-conceptualizations of classical works. Re-writings, reworkings, artistic depictions, stagings, etc., of Greek or Roman literature for popular audiences (including Nolan's recent film). Global receptions and performances of Greco-Roman literature for postcolonial or comparative literature purposes. Feminist performed engagement with and critique of classics. Dr. Phillip Zapkin Guest Editor Manuscript Submission Information Manuscripts should be submitted online at www.mdpi.com by registering and logging in to this website. Once you are registered, click here to go to the submission form. Manuscripts can be submitted until the deadline. All submissions that pass pre-check are peer-reviewed. Accepted papers will be published continuously in the journal (as soon as accepted) and will be listed together on the special issue website. Research articles, review articles as well as short communications are invited. For planned papers, a title and short abstract (about 250 words) can be sent to the Editorial Office for assessment. Submitted manuscripts should not have been published previously, nor be under consideration for publication elsewhere (except conference proceedings papers). All manuscripts are thoroughly refereed through a double-anonymized peer-review process. A guide for authors and other relevant information for submission of manuscripts is available on the Instructions for Authors page. Literature is an international peer-reviewed open access quarterly journal published by MDPI. Please visit the Instructions for Authors page before submitting a manuscript. The Article Processing Charge (APC) for publication in this open access journal is 1000 CHF (Swiss Francs). Submitted papers should be well formatted and use good English. Authors may use MDPI's English editing service prior to publication or during author revisions. Keywords: Greek Roman literature reception adaptation studies classics
